Ar_3051.t: Treatise on Variant Readings of the Qur'an (Kitab al-Badi') by Ibn Khalawayh (d. 980)
Ar_3051.c: Treatise on Variant Readings of the Qur'an (Kitab al-Badi') by Ibn Khalawayh (d. 980-1). Written in an elegant angular script, this work discusses different readings of the Qur'an, and was written by the grammarian and lexicographer Ibn Khalawayh. Born in Hamadan (Iran), he studied in Baghdad (Iraq), before moving to Aleppo (Syria), where he worked at the court of the Hamdanid amir Sayf al-Dawla. This copy of his book may have been written during Ibn Khalawayh's lifetime: an additional note records that the manuscript was written out in 370 AH (September-October 980). Codex, ink, pigments and gold on paper, 106 folios, Arabic text in eastern kufic script, Kitab al-Badi`, a treatise on canonical and non-canonical variant readings of the Qur'an, by Abu `Abdullah al-Husayn ibn Ahmad ibn Khalawayh (d. 370 AH, 980-981), composed for Sayf al-Dawla (r. 945-967), Hamdanid ruler of Aleppo, possibly copied in Syria, dated Rabi` I 370H (folio 106r: additional line in naskh), September-October 980

Ar_3113.t: Fatḥ al-muta`āl fī madḥ al-ni`āl, by al-Maqqarī (d. 1632)
Ar_3113.c: Treatise on the Prophet Muhammad's sandals (Fatḥ al-muta`āl fī madḥ al-ni`āl), by al-Maqqarī (d. 1632). Born in Tlemcen (Algeria), the scholar and historian Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad al-Maqqarī (d. 1632) lived in several different cities, serving the Sa`adi ruler Aḥmad al-Manṣūr (d. 1603) in Fez and Marrakesh, before moving to Cairo, c. 1617. Composed in 1621, this work discusses the Prophet's sandals and also the traces of his footprints, which are attested in different sacred locations. This manuscript was copied in May 1661 from al-Maqqari's original autograph manuscript, which he had written out in 1632 (most likely in Cairo). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 121 folios, leather binding, Arabic text in naskh script, with 6 diagrams of the Prophet's sandal outline, Fatḥ al-muta`āl fī madḥ al-ni`āl by Shihāb al-Dīn Abū al-`Abbās Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn al-Ṭaṭā’ūnī al-Maqqarī al-Tilimsānī al-Mālikī al-Ash`arī (1578-1632), copied by `Abd al-Fattāḥ al-Ashmūnī al-Shāfi`ī, from an autograph

Ar_3315.c: Kitāb al-Fihrist, by Ibn al-Nadīm (d. 990). This is an important early copy of the renowned Fihrist by Ibn al-Nadīm (d. 990), a comprehensive catalogue of all known authors whose books were available to interested readers in late tenth-century Baghdad. Probably from Mosul in northern Iraq, the author was a book-dealer (warrāq) based in Baghdad. He compiled his encyclopaedic account of Arabic written culture over many years, gathering biographical information on authors and listing their known works, ordered by topic, over ten chapters (interchangeably called maqāla or juz’ in this copy). Ibn al-Nadīm completed his great bio-bibliographical work in 987-988 (377H). The unidentified scribe of this manuscript checked and corrected it against the author’s original autograph copy (in the author’s hand, bi-khaṭṭ al-muṣannif), probably in Baghdad. Ar_3424.t: Revision of Euclid's Elements of Geometry (Islah al-ustuqusat)
a: `Ali ibn `Umar ibn `Ali al-Qazwini; Athir al-Din al-Mufaddal ibn `Umar al-Abhari
Ar_3424.c: Revision of Euclid's Elements of Geometry (Islah al-ustuqusat) by al-Abhari. Codex, ink and pigments on paper, 126 folios, Arabic text in ta`liq script, mathematical diagrams in red, Islah al-ustuqusat, revised translation of Euclid's Elements of Geometry, by Athir al-Din al-Mufaddal ibn `Umar al-Abhari (d. 1265), manuscript copied by `Ali ibn `Umar ibn `Ali al-Qazwini (d. 1276), Iran or Iraq, undated, c. 1250-1275.

Ar_3491.t: Kitāb al-`ilm, by Abū Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Ḥarb al-Nasā’ī (d. 849)
a: `Abdullāh ibn `Alī ibn `Umar ibn Shibl al-Ḥimyarī al-Ṣanhājī
`Abdullāh ibn `Alī ibn `Umar ibn Shibl al-Ḥimyarī al-Ṣanhājī
Ar_3491.c: Kitāb al-`ilm, by Abū Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Ḥarb al-Nasā’ī (d. 849). Codex, ink on paper, textile-wrapped bookbinding, 12 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Kitāb al-`ilm, by Abū Khaythama Zuhayr ibn Ḥarb al-Nasā’ī al-Shaybānī (d. 849), collection of Hadith Traditions about acquiring and sharing knowledge, copied by `Abdullāh ibn `Alī ibn `Umar ibn Shibl al-Ḥimyarī al-Ṣanhājī (d. 1324), undated, c. 1250-1324.

Ar_3541.t: The greater consideration (al-Ri`ayat al-kubra), by Ibn Hamdan (d. 1295)
Ar_3541.c: The greater consideration (al-Ri`ayat al-kubra), by Ibn Hamdan (d. 1295). Codex, ink on paper, 279 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, al-Ri`ayat al-Kubra, by Najm al-Din Abu `Abdullah Ahmad ibn Hamdan ibn Shabib al-Harrani al-Hanbali (d. 1295, Cairo), second volume of his treatise on Hanbali jurisprudence, probably Cairo, Egypt, dated Wednesday 16 Rabi` II 706H, 25 October 1306.

Ar_3714.c: al-Fuṣūl al-ḥikmīya, by al-Fārābī (d. 950). Codex, ink and colour on paper, 30 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Selected Aphorisms (al-Fuṣūl al-ḥikmīya, also titled al-Fuṣūl al-muntaza`a min aqāwīl al-qudamā’ fī tadbīr al-mudun), by Abū Naṣr al-Fārābī (d. 950), political writings linked with ancient Greek philosophers, copied by Ibrāhīm ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā, Damanhur, Egypt, dated Sunday 11 Rabi` I 704H, 12 October 1304.

Ar_3722.t: History of Jedda (Kitab al-jawahir al-mu'adda fi ta'rikh Jadda), by Ahmad al-Hadrawi (d. 1909)
a: Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ahmad al-Hadrawi al-Hashimi al-Makki
Ar_3722.c: History of Jedda (Kitab al-jawahir al-mu'adda fi ta'rikh Jadda), by Ahmad al-Hadrawi (d. 1909). Describing the city of Jedda (in modern Saudi Arabia), this manuscript was copied out by its author, writing in Mecca, in 1871. Codex, ink and pigments on paper, 34 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, al-Jawahir al-mu`adda fi ta'rikh Jadda, history and topography of Jedda, by Ahmad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ahmad al-Hadrawi al-Hashimi al-Makki (1836-1909), autograph manuscript, Mecca, Saudi Arabia, dated 1288H, 1871.

Ar_3751.t: Forty key points on the principles of religion (Lubab al-arba'in fi usul al-din), by Siraj al-Din al-Urmawi (d. 1283)
Ar_3751.c: Forty key points on the principles of religion (Lubab al-arba'in fi usul al-din), by Siraj al-Din al-Urmawi (d. 1283). This text consists of forty epitomes, or condensed summaries, of Fakhr al-Din al-Razi's theology manual, al-Mabahith al-`arba`un fi usul al-din. The author, Siraj al-Din al-Urmawi (d. 1283) was born in Urumiya (Iran), and worked in Mosul (Iraq), Cairo (Egypt) and finally Konya (Turkey). Codex, ink on paper, 152 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Forty key points on the principles of religion (Lubab al-arba'in fi usul al-din), by Siraj al-Din Abu'l-Thana' Mahmud ibn Abi Bakr al-Urmawi (1198-1283), condensed epitome of al-Mabahith al-`arba`un fi usul al-din, theology manual by Fakhr al-Din al-Razi (d. 1209), copied by `Umar ibn Ahmad al-Mutatabbib, possibly Konya, Turkey, dated Dhu'l-Qa`da 704H, 1305.

Ar_3764.t: Intikhāb uṣūl al-samā`āt, volume 3, by al-Silafī (d. 1180)
a: Abū al-Ṭāhir Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Silafī al-Isbahānī al-Jarwānī
Abū al-Ṭāhir Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Silafī al-Isbahānī al-Jarwānī
Ar_3764.c: Intikhāb uṣūl al-samā`āt, volume 3, by al-Silafī (d. 1180). Codex, ink on paper, textile-wrapped bookbinding, 9 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Intikhāb uṣūl al-samā`āt, volume 3, by Abū al-Ṭāhir Aḥmad ibn Muḥammad ibn Aḥmad al-Silafī al-Isbahānī al-Jarwānī (d. 1180), extracts from the teachings of Abū al-Ḥasan `Alī ibn al-Musharraf al-Ḥusayn ibn al-Musallam `Umar ibn al-Farrā’ al-Mawṣilī al-Miṣrī (d. 1125), author’s autograph copy, Alexandria, Egypt, dated Sha`ban 513H, November 1119.

Ar_3806.c: Hadith Traditions, collected by al-Kaḥḥāl (d. 1092). Codex, ink on paper, modern binding, 10 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Hadith Traditions collected by Abū al-Faḍl Ja`far ibn Yaḥyā ibn Ibrāhīm ibn Yaḥyā ibn `Abdullāh al-Makkī al-Kaḥḥāl (d. 1092), unsigned, undated, c. 1100-1200, with many audition notes, one (fol. 10r) signed `Alī ibn `Uthmān ibn Ibrāhīm ibn al-Turkumānī al-Māridīnī (d. 1349) and dated 5 Dhu’l-Qa`da 708H, 16 April 1309.

Ar_3831.c: On falconry (Kitab al-bayzara), by the Fatimid caliph's court falconer. Produced under the Fatimid dynasty in Cairo, this treatise covers both falconry and hunting: like most rulers, the patron Caliph al-`Aziz billah (r. 975-996) was known to enjoy hunting, archery and polo. The text discusses first-hand knowledge of hunting practices, and also adds poetry and anecdotes on the same subject. The author was the Caliph's court falconer, `Abdullah al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Bazyar: he drew extensively from another work, Kitab al-masayid wa'l-matarid written by the poet Kushajim (d. 970), who is not credited. Codex, ink on paper, 154 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with headings in red, Kitab al-Bayzara, treatise on falconry and hunting, incomplete text, produced for Fatimid caliph al-`Aziz (r. 975-996) by his chief falconer (bazyar) `Abdullah al-Hasan ibn al-Husayn al-Bazyar, unsigned, undated, possibly c. 975.

Ar_3838.t: Charming anecdotes on admonition regarding honourable people with physical blights (al-Nukat al-ziraf fi al-maw'iza bi-dhawi al-`ahat min al-ashraf), by Jar Allah ibn Fahd (1486-1547)
a: Jar Allah Muhammad ibn `Abd al-`Aziz ibn `Umar ibn Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Najm al-Din Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Khayr Muhammad ibn Muhammad `Abdullah ibn Fahd al-Hashimi al-Makki al-Shafi`i
Jar Allah Muhammad ibn `Abd al-`Aziz ibn `Umar ibn Taqi al-Din Muhammad ibn Najm al-Din Muhammad ibn Abi'l-Khayr Muhammad ibn Muhammad `Abdullah ibn Fahd al-Hashimi al-Makki al-Shafi`i
Ar_3838.c: Charming anecdotes on admonition regarding honourable people with physical blights (al-Nukat al-ziraf fi al-maw'iza bi-dhawi al-`ahat min al-ashraf), by Jar Allah ibn Fahd (1486-1547). This is the only surviving copy of Jar Allah's third revision (in 1543) of his controversial book of anecdotes about important and honourable people with various disabilities and other physical conditions and characteristics. The Arabic term `ahat refers not only to physical disabilities inherited or caused by disease or injury (such as blindness and paralysis) but also physical conditions such as baldness. Historically, there are different genres of Arabic literature dealing with `ahat, including legal judgements, consolation and humour. In this case, the author caused great offence in his home city of Mecca with the first version of this book, in which he named several contemporary luminaries as bald. Ar_3927.t: Qisṭās al-mu`ādala fī `ilm al-jabr wa al-muqābala, by al-Zanjānī (d. 1262)
Ar_3927.c: Qisṭās al-mu`ādala fī `ilm al-jabr wa al-muqābala, by al-Zanjānī (d. 1262). Codex, ink and colour on paper, modern buckram bookbinding, 226 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, Qisṭās al-mu`ādala fī `ilm al-jabr wa al-muqābala, by `Abd al-Wahhāb ibn Ibrahīm `Abd al-Wahhāb al-Zanjānī (d. 1262), on solving equations in algebra, colophon dated Thursday 28 Muharram 643H, 25 June 1245 (but transcribed from earlier reference copy cross-checked by the author in Tabriz), copied by `Alī Naqī al-Abharī, Iran, undated, c. 1500-1600.

Ar_3968.t: Collection (majmū`) of 3 texts, by al-Tanūkhī (d. 1245) and Yaḥyā
a: Muḥammad ibn `Alī ibn Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr al-Yamanī
Muḥammad ibn `Alī ibn Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr al-Yamanī
Ar_3968.c: Collection (majmū`) of 3 texts, by al-Tanūkhī (d. 1245) and Yaḥyā. Codex, ink and colour on paper, modern buckram bookbinding, 60 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, collection (majmū`) of 3 texts, (1: fols. 1-21) al-Anwār al-muqtabasa min uwār al-nār, by Amīn al-Dīn Abū al-Faḍl `Abd al-Muḥsin ibn Ḥammūd al-Tanūkhī al-Ḥalabī (Mamluk minister, d. 1245), anthology of poetry about fire, read aloud to the author at a scholarly gathering (halaqa) in Damascus mosque, (2: fols. 22-58) Mukhtār min Kitāb al-Ḥadā’iq, anonymous collection of letters by famous people, possibly an extract from Ḥadā’iq al-wasā’il ilā ṭuruq al-rasā’il by al-Bayhaqī (d. 1169), (3: fols. 59-60) Ḥall abyāt Ibn al-Rūmī, by Muḥyī al-Dīn Abū al-Faḍl Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad ibn Yaḥyā ibn Muḥammad ibn `Alī, commentary on 3 verses from the Dīwān of Ibn al-Rūmī (d. 896), 3 different copyists, (1) copied by Muḥammad ibn `Alī ibn Muḥammad ibn Manṣūr al-Yamanī, (2) and (3) unsigned, (1) Damascus, Syria, (1) dated Thursday 13 Dhu’l-Hi

Ar_3999.t: Collection (majmū`) of 6 texts on grammar and logic, by Tha`lab (d. 904), Ibn Fāris (d. c. 1005), al-`Askarī (d. 1005), al-Dashtakī (d. 1542), al-Kātibī (d. 1276) and al-Dawwānī (d. 1501)
Ar_3999.c: Collection (majmū`a) of 6 texts on grammar and logic, by Tha`lab (d. 904), Ibn Fāris (d. c. 1005), al-`Askarī (d. 1005), al-Dashtakī (d. 1542), al-Kātibī (d. 1276) and al-Dawwānī (d. 1501). Ar_4019.t: The Sources of Truths and the Explication of Paths (`Uyūn al-ḥaqā’iq wa īḍāḥ al-ṭarā’iq), by Abū al-Qāsim al-`Irāqī (d. c. 1280)
Ar_4019.c: The Sources of Truths and the Explication of Paths (`Uyūn al-ḥaqā’iq wa īḍāḥ al-ṭarā’iq), by Abū al-Qāsim al-`Irāqī (d. c. 1280). A compendium on magic, alchemy and esoteric "sacred secrets" (nawamis), the author outlines the contents as follows: "all the operations of sacred secrets, fire spells, suffumigations, fermentations, soporifics, invisibility spells, hiding spells, cunning works, and the occult properties of minerals, plants, animals and the condition of man's composition and what relates to him in all seasons". Codex, ink and colours on paper, 70 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with diagrams and images, The Sources of Truths and the Explication of Paths (`Uyūn al-ḥaqā’iq wa īḍāḥ al-ṭarā’iq), by Abū al-Qāsim al-`Irāqī, known as al-Sīmāwī (d. c. 1280), text on alchemy, magic and occult science, unsigned, possibly Syria, undated, c. 1600-1700.

Ar_4163.t: Āthār al-bilād wa akhbār al-`ibād, by Zakariyya al-Qazvīnī (d. 1283)
Ar_4163.c: Monuments of the lands and the annals of God's servants (Āthār al-bilād wa akhbār al-`ibād), by Zakariyya ibn Muḥammad ibn Maḥmūd al-Qazvīnī (1203-1283). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 182 folios, painted, gilded and moulded leather binding, Arabic text in naskh script, with illuminated title page (chahar lawh, fols. 1v-2r) and chapter headings (sarlawh, fols. 21r, 39v, 146v 170r,179r), and linear map diagrams (fols. 4r world map, 33r the Ka`ba sanctuary, 42r the Alexandria lighthouse, 51r the Nile Delta, 128v map of Qazvin, 177v map of Istanbul), Monuments of the lands and the annals of God's servants (Āthār al-bilād wa akhbār al-`ibād), by Zakariyya ibn Muḥammad ibn Maḥmūd al-Qazvīnī (1203-1283), geography treatise organised in chapters for the seven climes (world regions), signed Ibrahim, Iran or Iraq, dated (colophon, fol. 182r), 19 Jumada II 742H, 30 November 1341.

Ar_4169.t: al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya, by al-Būṣīrī (d. 1294), combined with Takhmīs al-Burda, by al-Fayyūmī
Ar_4169.c: al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya, by al-Būṣīrī (d. 1294), combined with Takhmīs al-Burda, by al-Fayyūmī. Al-Būṣīrī’s poem in praise of the Prophet was widely admired in Mamluk society. This manuscript was made for Yashbak min Mahdī, who held the office of grand secretary (Dawādār Kabīr) to Sultan Qaytbay (r. 1468-1496). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather binding, 29 folios, Arabic text in naskh and thuluth scripts, with illuminated title page (sarlawh, shamsa, fol. 1r) and colophon (shamsa, fol. 29r), Pearly Stars in Praise of the Finest of Creation (al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya), also known as the Poem of the Cloak or Mantle Ode (Qaṣīdat al-Burda) by Sharaf al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd al-Būṣīrī al-Ṣanhājī (Imam al-Būṣīrī, d. 1294-7), poem in praise of the Prophet, combined with the Amplification (Takhmīs al-Burda, explanatory text) by Nāṣir al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn `Abd al-Samad al-Makkī al-Fayyūmī, produced for Amir Yashbak min Mahdī (Dawādār Ka

Ar_4177.t: al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya, by al-Būṣīrī (d. 1294), combined with Takhmīs al-Burda, by al-Fayyūmī
Ar_4177.c: al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya, by al-Būṣīrī (d. 1294), combined with Takhmīs al-Burda, by al-Fayyūmī. The Poem of the Cloak (Qaṣīdat al-Burda) was composed by the Mamluk poet al-Būṣīrī in honour of the Prophet. Later, other poets wrote new lines which rhymed with the original verses, and amplified their meaning. The large calligraphy here is al-Būṣīrī’s poem, and the smaller red and black text is the second poet’s composition. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 29 folios, leather bookbinding, Arabic text in naskh and thuluth scripts, with illuminated double page with titles (double frontispiece with 12-sided star polygon on each side, fols. 1v-2r), Pearly Stars in Praise of the Finest of Creation (al-Kawākib al-durriyya fī madḥ khayr al-bariyya), also known as the Poem of the Cloak or Mantle Ode (Qaṣīdat al-Burda) by Sharaf al-Dīn Muḥammad ibn Saʿīd al-Būṣīrī al-Ṣanhājī (Imam al-Būṣīrī, d. 1294-7), poem in praise of the Prophet, combined with the Amplification (Ta

Ar_4180.c: Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, volumes 1 and 15. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding with blind-tooled and gold design, dark green silk doublures, 76 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with two illuminated frontispieces (title cartouche with medallion fol. 2r, pointed medallion fol. 40r), al-Jāmi` al-Ṣaḥīḥ (al-Jāmi` al-musnad as-ṣaḥīḥ al-mukhtasar), volumes 15 (fols. 1-39) and 1 (fols. 40-76), by Abū Abdullāh Muḥammad ibn Ismā`īl al-Bukhārī (810-870), compilation of Ḥadīth Traditions, assembled from separately-bound volumes of same thirty-volume set, fol. 40 is from volume 8, two unsigned colophons (fol. 36r, 76v), probably Syria, undated, c. 1340-1360.

Ar_4183.t: Counsels for Alexander (Nasayih Iskandar) by pseudo-Aristotle
Ar_4183.c: Counsels for Alexander (Nasayih Iskandar) by pseudo-Aristotle. Codex, ink, gold and pigment on paper, Arabic text in ta`liq script, signed by Ja`far al-Baysunghuri, Herat, Afghanistan, dated 829H, 1425-1426. This is an abbreviated version of the pseudo-Aristotelian 'Politics', known as in Arabic as Sirr al-Asrar (Secret of Secrets): the text is presented in the form of letters written by Aristotle to his pupil, Alexander the Great, while Alexander was engaged in the conquest of Iran. Produced in Herat for the Timurid prince Baysunghur (d. 1433), the manuscript belongs to an important category of wisdom literature, designed to educate princes in statecraft and political vision. This is one of at least three manuscripts in the Chester Beatty collection known to be produced in Baysunghur's renowned court atelier.

Ar_4199.t: Prayers for the week, attributed to `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (d. 661)
Ar_4199.c: Prayers for the week, attributed to `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (d. 661). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, painted lacquer covers, 16 folios, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script, with full page illumination (fol. 1r), gold backdrop (fols. 1v-2r) and gold headings with spiral scrollwork (sarlawh, throughout), Prayers for the seven days of the week, attributed (on fol. 1v) to `Alī ibn Abī Ṭālib (d. 661), possibly Istanbul, Turkey, undated, c. 1450-1500.

Ar_4203.t: al-Shifā’ fī ta`rīf ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā, volume 20, by Qāḍī ‘Iyāḍ (d. 1149)
Ar_4203.c: al-Shifā’ fī ta`rīf ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā, volume 20, by Qāḍī ‘Iyāḍ (d. 1149). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 55 folios, leather bookbinding with blind-tooling, gold detail and block-printing (on doublures), Arabic text in naskh script, with illuminated title page (fol. 1r), and alternating folio colour (light orange paper every 2-3 folios, throughout), al-Shifā’ fī ta`rīf ḥuqūq al-Muṣṭafā, volume 20, by Abū al-Faḍl `Iyāḍ ibn Mūsā al-Yaḥṣubī al-Sabtī (1083-1149), account of the Prophet's life, habits, sayings and character, compiled from different Hadith authorities, unsigned, possibly Cairo, Egypt, undated, c. 1350-1370, with additional audition note (fol. 55v) authorised (ijāzā) by al-Shaykh Sharaf al-Dīn, signed by Muḥammad ibn Muḥammad al-khaṭīb al-Ḥanafī, dated 25 Ramadan 771H, April 1370.

Ar_4204.t: Bānat Su`ād, by Ka`b ibn Zuhayr
Ar_4204.c: Bānat Su`ād, by Ka`b ibn Zuhayr. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 17 folios, leather bookbinding with gold detail, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script, with illuminated medallion (fol. 1r), Bānat Su`ād, by Abū al-Miḍrab Ka`b ibn Zuhayr ibn Abī Sulmā al-Muzanī al-Muḍariyya, poem (qaṣīda) in praise of the Prophet, dedicated to (bi-rasm, fol. 1r) `Āmir ibn `Abd al-Wahhāb (r. 1489-1517, Ṭāhirid sultan of Yemen), copied by Maḥmūd bin Muḥammad al-Shīrāzī, probably Shiraz, Iran, dated (fol. 17r) 920H, 1514-1515. The illumination around the dedication (fol. 1r) is stylistically consistent with Shiraz production, which corresponds with the calligrapher's name (al-Shīrāzī) in his signature on the final folio (fol. 17r). However, seen under transmitted light, the paper of folio 17 is different to the rest of this manuscript: the central text area is darker paper of a different colour and the ink a darker blue, while the outer borders are of the same paper as the rest of the codex. Ar_4222.t: Book of the constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita), by `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986)
Ar_4222.c: Book of the constellations (Kitāb ṣuwar al-kawākib al-thābita), by `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986). For many centuries, astronomers in west Asia retained, reviewed and revised inherited scientific models, but kept an open mind. In this book on the constellations, for example, the Iranian astronomer `Abd al-Raḥmān al-Ṣūfī (d. 986, Baghdad) referred carefully to the star catalogue recorded by Ptolemy in the second century AD (Ptolemy in turn drew from his own predecessors), and also compared that scientific system to the star-names used in Arab folk astronomy. Al-Ṣūfī's book discussed the forty-eight "classical" constellations (including the Zodiac constellations), recorded their celestial longitude and latitude positions (in the star tables here), and provided two mirror-images of each constellation. Ar_4223.t: Guide to Happiness (Dalā'il al-khayrāt) by Shaykh al-Jazūlī (d. 1465)
a: Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn `Abd al-Rahman al-Riyahi
Ar_4223.c: Guide to Happiness (Dalā'il al-khayrāt) by Shaykh al-Jazūlī (d. 1465). This prayer book was originally composed in Morocco, by the Sufi scholar Muḥammad al-Jazūlī (d. 1465). Later copies were produced from North Africa to India, and usually contain illustrations linked to the life and memory of the Prophet Muḥammad. In this example dated 1638-39 (1048H), there are schematic diagrams of the Ka`ba shrine in Mecca (3v), the Prophet's home and tomb in Medina (4r), and the sacred outline of his sandal (2v-3r). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 93 folios, Arabic text in maghribi script, with diagrams of holy names, the Prophet’s footprint, and the holy sites in Mecca and Medina (fols. 1v-4r), and full page illumination (fols. 4v-5v, 93v), Guide to Happiness and the Shinings of Lights, for reciting the prayer to bless the chosen Prophet (Dalā'il al-khayrāt wa shawāriq al-anwār fī dhikr al-ṣalāt ‘ala Nabī al-Mukhtar), by Abū `Abdullāh Muḥammad ibn Sulaymān ibn Abī Bakr al-Jazūlī al-Simlān

Ar_5232.t: Sublime Methods in Spiritual Devices (al-Ṭuruq al-saniyya fī al-ālāt al-ruḥāniyya), by Taqī al-Dīn (1526-1585)
Ar_5232.c: Sublime Methods in Spiritual Devices (al-Ṭuruq al-saniyya fī al-ālāt al-ruḥāniyya), by Taqī al-Dīn (1526-1585). Taqī al-Dīn was a renowned scientist, who worked in Ottoman Egypt and Syria, and later at the imperial capital of Istanbul, where he built an observatory. Organised in six chapters, this treatise is about hydraulic engineering, and describes machines for lifting weights, raising water, playing musical instruments, and irrigation, as well as water clocks (clepsydras) and a self-moving spit operated by a steam turbine. Codex, ink and colours on paper, 44 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with headings in red, and mechanical diagrams (up to fol. 26v, with blank spaces thereafter), Sublime Methods in Spiritual Devices (al-Ṭuruq al-saniyya fī al-ālāt al-ruḥāniyya), by Taqī al-Dīn Abū Bakr Muhammad ibn Qādhī Ma’rūf ibn Ahmad al-Shāmī al-‘Asadī al-Rāsid (1526-1585), on hydraulic engineering, identified as autograph copy, possibly Cairo, Egypt, undated, c. 1550.

Ar_5655.t: Nihāyat al-su’l wa al-umniyya fī ta‘allum ‘amāl al-furūsiyya, by al-Aqṣarā’ī (d. 1348)
Ar_5655.c: Manual on the Arts of Horsemanship (Nihāyat al-su’l wa al-umniyya fī ta‘allum ‘amāl al-furūsiyya) by al- Aqṣarā’ī (d. 1348). First composed in Mamluk Damascus, al- Aqṣarā’ī's well-known military encyclopaedia describes the many skills required for an effective cavalry army, organised in twelve lessons. There is an extensive Arabic literature on the arts of horsemanship, and this copy (probably made in Damascus, in 1366) is one of the earliest illustrated examples known. These arts include the care and training of horses, the correct handling of weapons, and equestrian parade displays for the hippodrome, as well as cavalry formations in battle, just distribution of war booty, and treaty negotiations. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 319 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, illuminated frontispiece (fol. 1r), with seven paintings (fols. 120v, 130r, 151v, 154v, 157v, 166r, faces later re-painted) and seven diagrams (fols. 109v-113), Nihāyat al-su’l wa al-umniyya fī ta‘allum ‘amāl al

Arm_558.c: Codex manuscript containing a Gospel book written on paper in Armenian in a bologir (cursive miniscule) script, made for the Patriarch of the Armenian Church, Constantine I (1221-1267) between 1248 and 1267 and attributed to the illuminator Kirakos (active 1239-1267), probably at Hromkla (modern Turkey). It was acquired by Beatty from the London-based dealer, William H. Robinson, in May 1947. This manuscript is an outstanding example of thirteenth-century art from the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia (1099–1375), situated in the southeast of modern Turkey. It was prepared for the Catholicos Constantine I (1221–1267), Patriarch of the Armenian Church. Constantine was a leading patron of the arts and this gospel book was probably produced at Hromkla, capital of his patriarchal see. The illumination is attributed to the artist Kirakos and displays a remarkable amalgamation of Byzantine and Islamic ornament. Arm_558_f_15.t: St Matthew from a Gospel book
Arm_558_f_15.c: Folio from a Gospel book written on paper in Armenian, made for the Patriarch of the Armenian Church, Constantine I (1221-1267), between 1248 and 1267 and attributed to the illuminator Kirakos (active 1239-1267), probably at Hromkla, in the Armenian kingdom of Cilicia. Matthew the Evangelist wears a blue tunic and light purple mantle. He sits at a desk, with golden background, writing in a book held by his symbol (a winged man). The blue text reads 'Saint Matthew'. The folio is blank on the recto.

Arm_564.c: Armenian Gospel book on paper with canon tables, gospel prefaces and portraits of the Evangelists, written by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in bolorgir script in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet, and bound in a blind-tooled brown leather cover (traces of metal crosses) with three straps, and textile board linings. The manuscript was later taken to Isfahan (folios 258-269 were added by Aton), where it was repaired in 1667 during the patriarchate at Etchmiadzin of the Catholicos Jacob IV (Հակոբ Դ Ջուղայեցի). A catalogue dedication is written on the inside cover by the Armenian Patriarch of Constantinople Malachia Ormanian (1896–1908). The first letter of each Gospel is formed by the symbol of the Evangelist and the first line is written in zoomorphic or floral letters. Several folios (and therefore important iconographic scenes) are missing from the first quire. Marginal ornament consists primarily of floral scrolls with the occasional birds, sirens, quadrupeds, figure

Arm_564_f_01.t: The Presentation in the Temple (recto, above), The Baptism (recto, below) and The Transfiguration (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_01.c: Folio from the preface of an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the Presentation in the Temple (upper register) and the Baptism (lower register), with the Transfiguration on the verso. Inscriptions identify the paintings as 'The bringing to the temple on the fortieth day', 'Baptism', and 'The Transfiguration of our Saviour on mount Thabor'. The Presentation is divided into two arches. On the left are Mary and Joseph and on the right are the Prophetess Anna and Simeon who holds the baby. In the Baptism, Jesus stands in the Jordan River flanked by the larger John the Baptist wearing a camel cloak on the left and an angel on the right; the Holy Spirit as a dove appears above. In the Transfiguration 'Jesus Christ' stands on a mountain enclosed in a starry mandorla and flanked by 'Elijah' and 'Moses.' This vision is witnessed by 'the disciples Peter, James, and John, sons of Z

Arm_564_f_02.t: The Raising of Lazarus (recto, above), the Entry into Jerusalem (recto, below), the Washing of the Feet (verso (above), and Communion of the Apostles (verso, below), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_02.c: Folio from the preface of an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto are the Raising of Lazarus (upper register) and the Entry into Jerusalem (lower register), and on the verso is Jesus Washing his Disciples' Feet (upper register) and the Communion of Apostles (lower register). Inscriptions identify the scenes as 'the raising of Lazarus', 'the arrival on the ass', 'the washing of the feet', and 'the mass in the upper chamber'. In the Raising of Lazarus, sisters Mary and Martha kneel before Jesus in front of the open tomb of Lazarus (foreshadowing the Resurrection). The Entry into Jerusalem combines two events. The small figure in the tree is identified as ‘Zacchaeus’, a wealthy tax collector in Jericho who climbed a sycamore tree to see Jesus over the crowd (Gospel of Luke only). After leaving Jericho, Jesus travelled onto Jerusalem on a colt or donkey. The awaiting crowd spread

Arm_564_f_03.t: The Pentecost (recto) and Letter of Eusebius (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_03.c: Folio from the preface of an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is a painting of the Pentecost. Under a rainbow extending from the beak of the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove are the apostles seated in two groups above an arched opening; below are three figures, the central one crowned and holding a lance (the personification of Kosmos). An inscription identifies the scene as 'the descent of the Holy Spirit on the holy apostles'. A red seal from Ortaköy in Istanbul is stamped in the lower margin. On the verso is the beginning of the Letter of Eusebius within an architectural frame, with a portrait of Eusebius holding a scroll in the decorated heading. A peacock and other birds are depicted around the frame.

Arm_564_f_04.t: Letter of Eusebius (recto) and Incomplete Canon Table (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_04.c: Folio from the preface of an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the end of the Letter of Eusebius within an architectural frame, with a portrait of Carpianus holding a scroll in the decorated heading. A peacock and other birds are depicted around the frame. On the verso is the beginning of the Canon Tables, the architectural frame and decorated heading are completed but the columns were left blank.

Arm_564_f_07.t: Incomplete Canon Table (recto) and Portrait of St Matthew (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_07.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the end of the Canon Tables, the architectural frame and decorated heading surrounded by birds and a tree are completed but the columns were left blank. On the verso is a seated portrait of the grey-bearded St Matthew in the act of writing his Gospel with a pen and a tablet resting on his lap; his symbol (a winged man) appears in the upper left corner.

Arm_564_f_08.t: Beginning of the Gospel of St Matthew, from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_08.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the beginning of the Gospel of Matthew with decorated heading, a floral design in the right margin and sirens above. The first letter of the Gospel (Գ) is formed by the symbol of the Evangelist (a winged man) holding a book; the rest of the letters in the first line are written in floral script. The Gospel continues on the verso in bolorgir script with verse initials in red erkat'agir script.

Arm_564_f_84.t: Preface to the Gospel of Mark (recto) and Portrait of St Mark (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_84.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the end of the preface to the Gospel of Mark written in bolorgir script. On the verso is a seated portrait of the bearded St Mark deep in thought, pens, ink pots and an open scroll before him; his symbol (a winged lion) holding a book appears in the upper right corner.

Arm_564_f_85.t: Beginning of the Gospel of St Mark, from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_85.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the beginning of the Gospel of Mark with decorated heading, a floral design in the right margin. The first line of the Gospel (Սկիզբն) is written in zoomorphic letters, formed by the symbol of the Evangelist (lions). The Gospel continues on the verso in bolorgir script with verse initials in red erkat'agir script.

Arm_564_f_134.t: Preface to the Gospel of St Luke (recto) and Portrait of St Luke (verso), from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_134.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the end of the preface to the Gospel of Luke written in bolorgir script. On the verso is a seated portrait of the bearded St Luke in the act of dipping his pen in an ink pot, the first lines of his Gospel already written on a scroll held in his other hand; his symbol (a winged ox) holding a book appears in the upper right corner.

Arm_564_f_135.t: Beginning of the Gospel of St Luke, from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_135.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the beginning of the Gospel of Luke with decorated heading, a floral design in the right margin with a resting ox at its base. The first letter of the Gospel (Ք) is formed by the symbol of the Evangelist (winged ox) holding a book; the rest of the letters in the first line of text are also written in zoomorphic script (formed by oxen). The Gospel continues on the verso in bolorgir script.

Arm_564_f_212.t: Preface to the Gospel of St John (recto) and Portrait of St John and Prochorus (verso, from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_212.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the end of the preface to the Gospel of John written in bolorgir script. On the verso is a standing portrait of the grey-bearded St John dictating his Gospel to the seated, young scribe, Porchorus; the Evangelist's symbol (an eagle) holding a book hovers above. The hand of God appears from the upper left corner.

Arm_564_f_213.t: Beginning of the Gospel of St John, from a Gospel book
Arm_564_f_213.c: Folio from an Armenian Gospel book, written and illuminated by the priest Karapet in the fifteenth century in the region of Van for Simeon vardapet. On the recto is the beginning of the Gospel of John with decorated heading, a floral design in the right margin and birds above. The first letter of the Gospel (ի) is formed by the symbol of the Evangelist (an eagle) holding a book; the rest of the letters in the first line of text are also written in zoomorphic script (formed by eagles). The Gospel continues on the verso in bolorgir script with verse initials in red erkat'agir script.

Arm_566_f_03.t: The Annunciation (recto) and the Nativity (verso) from a Gospel book

Arm_568_f_01.t: The Baptism (recto) and the Presentation at the Temple (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_01.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). On the recto, Jesus is baptised by John the Baptist in the Jordan River. A dove descends from above as two angels watch. Fish are visible beneath the waves of the river. On the verso, May and Joseph, who stand on the left, present the infant Jesus to Simeon in the Temple, Anna the prophetess stands behind him. The paintings were mounted in a paper frame in the mid-twentieth century.

Arm_568_f_02.t: The Raising of Lazarus (recto) and the Entry into Jerusalem (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_02.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). On the recto, Jesus performs the miracle of the Raising of Lazarus from the dead, as a young man unwraps the shroud. Jesus is attended by nine of his disciples and Mary and Martha, sisters of Lazarus, embrace his feet. On the verso, Jesus rides a donkey into the gates of the city, followed by nine of his disciples. A young boy spreads a cloak along his path, and another cuts a branch from a palm tree. The paintings were mounted in a paper frame in the mid-twentieth century.

Arm_568_f_03.t: The Washing of the feet (recto) and the Arrest (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_03.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). On the recto, at the Last Supper Jesus washes Peter's feet who scratches his head in confusion while ten additional apostles are seated behind. On the verso, Jesus is arrested by soldiers carrying torches and swords. The paintings were mounted in a paper frame in the mid-twentieth century.

Arm_568_f_05.t: The Harrowing of Hell (recto) and the Women at the Tomb (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_05.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). This is one of fourteen folios removed from the manuscript and housed separately. The Harrowing of Hell (recto) shows Jesus (holding a cross staff) taking the hand of Adam. Eve and another woman stand behind Adam, with David, Solomon and John the Baptist behind Jesus. Below, demons are trapped beneath the broken doors of hell, fallen in the shape of a cross. In the Women at the Tomb (verso), three women, stand before an angel pointing to the empty tomb, the sleeping soldiers depicted at the bottom.

Arm_568_f_06.t: The Ascension (recto) and Pentecost (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_06.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). On the recto, Jesus in a mandorla supported by six angels, ascends into heaven. In the lower register, Mary stands in the centre flanked by the apostles. On the verso, the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, with two groups of three apostles on either side. Below, two other groups of three apostles flank a central doorway in which stands a young crowned figure, probably Kosmos. The paintings were mounted in a paper frame in the mid-twentieth century.

Arm_568_f_07.t: The Transfiguration (recto) and the Dormition of the Virgin (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_07.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). This is one of fourteen folios removed from the manuscript and housed separately. In the Transfiguration (recto), Jesus stands in a mandorla flanked by Elijah and Moses. Below are the apostles Peter, James and John who go to a mountain with Jesus to pray and see a vision of him in heavenly glory. In the Dormition of the Virgin (verso) the apostles are gathered around Mary's deathbed. In the foreground is a man known as Athonios or Jephonias whose hands were cut off by the archangel Michael when he attempted to turn over Mary's funeral bier. His hands were restored after asking for Mary's forgiveness. Jesus hovers above, holding his mother's soul.

Arm_568_f_08.t: The Last Judgment (recto) and the Letter of Eusebius (verso) from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_08.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). On the recto, the Last Judgement is presented in two registers with the twelve apostles sitting above, while angels weigh the souls of the deceased below. Demons attempt to tip the scales down. On the verso is the opening to the Letter of Eusebius, presented in an architectural frame and illuminated in the heading by a portrait of Eusebius surrounded by floral scrolls.

Arm_568_f_75.t: The Entry into Jerusalem from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_75.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). A folio of text from the Gospel of Mark. The recto includes an illumination within the text (Mark 21.2-6). The painting depicts the Entry into Jerusalem with Jesus sitting on a donkey followed by three apostles approaching the gates to the city. The text continues on the verso.

Arm_568_f_109.t: Portrait of St Mark the Evangelist from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_109.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). St Mark sits at a desk before a fish-shaped lectern, contemplating his writing. The hand of God appears from the upper right corner. The folio is blank on the recto. The portrait would have faced the opening page of the Gospel of Mark.

Arm_568_f_140.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). The folio is from the Gospel according to Mark. On the recto, a large floral interlace ornament illuminates the right margin.

Arm_568_f_220.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). The folio is from the Gospel of Luke. On the recto, a demon-headed bird is depicted in the right margin beside Luke 11.14, Jesus drives out a demon.

Arm_568_f_260.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). The folio is from the Gospel of Luke. On the recto, a large floral interlace ornament illuminates the right margin.

Arm_568_f_274.t: Portrait of St John the Evangelist and Prochoros from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_274.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). John the Evangelist stands dictating his gospel to the deacon Prochoros his scribe. The hand of God appears in the upper left corner. The Gospel of Mark concludes on the recto.

Arm_568_f_275.t: Title page of the Gospel of John from a Gospel book
Arm_568_f_275.c: Parchment folio from a Gospel book written and illuminated c. 1536 in the Suynik' province of Armenia for Esayi the 'great vardapet' (abbot). The opening page of the Gospel of John is illuminated with an ornamental heading enclosing a pair of crowned sirens and floral interlace running the length of the right margin. The first letter of the Gospel is formed by the symbol of the Evangelist (eagle) with the first line of text written in zoomorphic and floral interlace letters. The remaining lines of text are written in blue and gold Erkat'agir script. The text continues on the verso in Bolorgir script.

Arm_570.c: Armenian Gospel book with canon tables and Gospel prefaces written in bolorgir script on paper and illuminated by Bishop Yovsep' (of Khartis'ar) at the Monastery of Khartis'ar or Haghartsin in 1541, bound in a plain brown leather cover. Colophons are written on f.4r (a short prayer), ff.188v-191r (in the hand of the scribe), f. 190r (repair and rebinding at the Red Monastery in 1728), and f. 191v (dated 1822). The parchment fly leaves are from an older Gospel book written in erkat'agir script and likely added during the rebinding in 1728. The Letter of Eusebius, Canon Tables 1, 6 to 10 and the Portrait of Mark are missing. The remaining Canon Tables are enclosed in architectural frames with decorated headings and birds above. Each Gospel is introduced by a portrait of its author, the painted frame entirely filled with geometric patterns, stylised buildings and furniture. Matthew (f.4v) is seated writing his Gospel, his symbol in the upper right corner, Luke (f.93v) is also writing his

Arm_573_1.t: The Annunciation and Raising of Lazarus from a Gospel book
Arm_573_1.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Annunciation to Mary by the archangel. The inscription reads, ‘Gabriel announces to the Virgin Mary’. Mary holds a spindle, a reference to the thread she prepared for the Veil of the Temple. The inscribed above the right-hand scene, 'the Raising of Lazarus.' Jesus is accompanied by his apostles who are identified by their halos. Mary and Martha, the sisters of Lazarus of Bethany, are pictured at Christ’s feet. The stone has been removed from the tomb and the shroud partially unwrapped.

Arm_573_2.t: The Adoration of the Magi and the Transfiguration from a Gospel book
Arm_573_2.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Transfiguration of Christ, as noted in the text above. Jesus, presented by the white robe and within a mandorla, is flanked by Elijah on the left and Moses holding tablets on the right. The episode is witnessed by Peter, James and John who lie on the ground below overwhelmed by the vision, James shields his eyes. The Adoration of the Magi is illuminated on the right-hand page, the inscription reads ‘the birth of Jesus’. Mary lays on a couch next to the swaddled baby who is resting in a manger near a donkey and ox. The wise men, two wearing crowns, present their gifts, the third points to the star above Jesus’ head. Joseph appears in the lower left corner pointing to the mother and child while a shepherd plays the pipe in the opposite corner. A group of angels witness the scene from above

Arm_573_3.t: The Presentation and Baptism of Jesus from a Gospel book
Arm_573_3.c: Bi-folio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in bolorgir and erkat'agir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). On the left-hand page is the Presentation at the Temple of Jerusalem of the baby Jesus. The text above reads ‘The coming to the temple on the fortieth day’. Joseph holds two doves or pigeons which were presented to the temple at the Purification of Mary, performed at the same time. The baby is held by Simeon over an altar, foreshadowing his future sacrifice. Anna the prophetess stands behind them holding a scroll. On the right-hand page is the Baptism of Jesus (identified in the text above) by John the Baptist. Jesus stands waste deep in the river as the Holy Spirit descends in the form of a dove, identifying him as the Son of God. Two angels stand on the opposite shore to emphasise the importance of the scene. Fish are visible beneath the waves, as is the personification of the River Jordan, a figure

Arm_573_4.t: The Entry into Jerusalem and the Washing of Feet from a Gospel book
Arm_573_4.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Entry into Jerusalem, the inscription reads ‘it is Palm Sunday’. Jesus sits side-saddle on a donkey, accompanied by his haloed-apostles. They approach the city gate where two men welcome them. A small figure in the lower right lays clothing along the path, while another diminutive figure stands in a palm tree cutting fronds to place on the ground. The Washing of Feet is illustrated on the right-hand page, as noted in the text above. During the Last Supper, as a sign of humility and farewell, Jesus washed the feet of his apostles, here represented by Peter who scratches his head in confusion.

Arm_573_5.t: The Harrowing of Hell and the Last Judgement from a Gospel book
Arm_573_5.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Descent into Limbo, or 'the Harrowing of Hell', as noted in the text above. The doors of hell lies broken beneath Christ’s feet, a demon crushed beneath them. Christ takes Adam’s hand to guide him out of limbo. Two angels appear above Adam. On the right are John the Baptist, the Virgin Mary crowned as Queen of Heaven and probably King David who also wears a crown. The Last Judgement is illustrated on the right-hand page. In the upper part of the page, the 'Ancient of Days' is enthroned on the four apocalyptic beasts. He is flanked by the Virgin Mary and John the Baptist. Hanging from the frame are the scales to weigh the souls of the deceased. Two demons attempt to tip the balance. The Archangel Michael slays the devil and weighs souls. The inscription above reads, ‘The Ancient of Days s

Arm_573_6.t: The Crucifixion and Entombment from a Gospel book
Arm_573_6.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Crucifixion. The inscription reads, ‘In similitude to Christ the pelican pierced his side and revived his young; Christ pierced his side and redeemed us with his blood.’ The crucified Jesus is flanked by his mother, the Virgin Mary, and St John the apostle, angels weep in the upper corners. The sun and moon either side of the cross represent the eclipse said to have taken place during the crucifixion. The pelican and her young are perched at the top of the cross and the skull of Adam sits at its foot. The Entombment is illuminated on the right-hand page, the inscription reads ‘the burial of the Lord’. Jesus is wrapped in a burial shroud and carried by Nicodemus and Joseph of Arimathea. The Virgin Mary and another female disciple, likely Mary Magdalene, are also present. Two angels watch

Arm_573_7.t: The Ascension and Pentecost from a Gospel book
Arm_573_7.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The left-hand page depicts the Ascension of Christ to heaven, as the inscription reads. Christ, seated in a mandorla, is carried by two angels above a rainbow. Directly below Jesus is his mother, the Virgin Mary. She is flanked by the apostles. Pentecost is illustrated on the right-hand page. The inscription reads ‘The descent of the Holy Spirit’, which appears in the form of a dove. The apostles are presented in four groups of three across two registers. The crowned figure at the bottom is probably Cosmos, or the Universe, a representation of the peoples of the world.

Arm_573_8.t: The Eusebian letter from a Gospel book
Arm_573_8.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). Portraits of Eusebius and Carpianus are painted under pointed arches, with floral scrolls filling the spandrels. Birds are found in the upper and side margins with a tall palm tree filling the outer margins. The text is the Letter of Eusebius.

Arm_573_9.t: The canon tables from a Gospel book
Arm_573_9.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). The canon tables are written within architectural frames with central animal capitals, the upper parts decorated with interlacing motifs in bright colours on a gold ground. Birds flank a vessel above the frame and trees fill the outer margins of the two-page opening.

Arm_573_10.t: Opening to Matthew from a Gospel book
Arm_573_10.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir and Erkat-agir scripts, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). A portrait of Matthew the Evangelist faces the opening page of his gospel. An octagonal frame intertwines a rectangular one. Mathew sits in a chair, writing in an open book. An ornamental heading fills the top half of the opening page of the text, while an interlacing palmette runs the length of the right margin. Birds are painted in the upper margin. The first letter of the gospel is formed by the evangelist's symbol (a winged man), while the remainder of the first line is formed by anthropomorphic letters, followed by alternating lines of gold and blue script. The text continues on the verso of the right-hand page.

Arm_573_11.t: Opening to Mark from a Gospel book
Arm_573_11.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir and Erkat-agir scripts, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). A portrait of Mark the Evangelist faces the opening page of his gospel. Mark sits on a bench, writing in an open book. Additional writing tools sit on the desk. The hand of God appears from the upper right corner. An ornamental heading fills the top half of the opening page of the text, while an interlacing palmette runs the length of the right margin. Birds are found in the upper margin. The first letter of the gospel is formed by the evangelist's symbol (two winged lions), while the remainder of the first line is formed by zoomorphic letters, followed by alternating lines of gold and blue script. The text continues on the verso of the right-hand page.

Arm_573_12.t: Opening to Luke from a Gospel book
Arm_573_12.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in bolorgir and erkat'agir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). A portrait of St Luke faces the opening page of his gospel. Luke sits before an open book, his writing tools on the desk near his feet, while a ciborium-like construction rises above the fish-shaped lectern. An ornamental heading fills the top half of the opening page of the text, while an interlacing palmette runs the length of the right-hand margin. Birds are painted in the upper margin of both pages. The first letter of the gospel is formed by the evangelist's symbol (an ox), while the remainder of the first line is formed by floral letters, followed in alternating lines of gold and blue script. The text continues on the verso of the right-hand page.

Arm_573_13.t: Opening to John from a Gospel book
Arm_573_13.c: Bifolio from an illuminated Gospel book written in Armenian on paper in Bolorgir and Erkat-agir script, by the scribe and artist Martiros of Khizan in 1596 at Constantinople (Istanbul). A portrait of John the Evangelist dictating to Prochoros, while receiving inspiration from the 'hand of God', faces the opening page of his gospel. The hand of God appears from the upper right corner. An ornamental heading fills the top half of the page of the text, while an interlacing palmette runs the length of the right-hand margin. An eagle with a book in its beak is found in the upper margin. The first letter of the gospel is formed by the a large anthropomorphic letter topped by the evangelist's symbol (an eagle with halo), while the remainder of the first line is formed by zoomorphic letters, followed by alternating lines of gold and blue script. The text continues on the verso of the right-hand page.

Arm_578.c: Armenian Gospel book written in Isfahan in 1655 (year of the Armenians 1104) by Yakob (Hakob). The illumination was the work of Hayrapet and paid for by Khat'un Dsaghik with 10 gold pieces. The manuscript was commissioned for an Armenian man called Ter Grigor, originally from Khoshap (eastern Turkey). At the end of the manuscript, additional notes show the Gospel passing through generations of the same family, and pray for blessings on all of them. A beautiful example of 17th-century manuscript illumination from Isfahan. It is painted in rich, bright colours, with a predominance of blue, red, green, yellow and lilac. The miniaturist Hayrapet, who has painted his own portrait kneeling at the foot of the cross, opposite the owner of the manuscript (f.15v), was one of the leading artists of New Julfa (the Armenian quarter of Isfahan).

Arm_585.c: A parchment codex with tooled leather binding and textile board linings, preserving an Armenian Gospel book written in the 17th century in Greater Armenia. The end of the Gospel of John and colophon are missing. Folios 267 and 268 (John 1.1-15 and Luke 24) are later insertions from another manuscript. The book opens with a series of 16 full-page miniatures depicting scenes from the Nativity and the Passion, all on gold ground. Prefatory material includes the Letter of Eusebius and the Canon tables, each with ornamental headpieces, and decorated with trees, vases, birds, lions and monkeys. Each gospel is introduced by a portrait of the Evangelist--Matthew (f.34v), Mark (f.99v), Luke (f.145v) and John (f.215v)--and an ornamental headpiece. The first letter of each Gospel are formed by the symbol of the Evangelist, while the second line and the initials of the verses are in gold or blue erkat'agir script. Arm_630.c: Folio from an unknown Gospel book written in Armenian in the twelfth or thirteenth century. A scribe sits in a high-backed chair before an inlaid wooden table. He is dipping his large brush into a bowl. Perhaps he is preparing the surface of his sheet for writing. This is an unusual example of an evangelist portrait, appearing as it does within the text rather than at the beginning of his book. The text above is from John 12:18-24 (recto) and 24-26 (verso). Verse numbers are written in the left margin.

Arm_662.c: Gilt silver hinged book cover, with cloisonné enamel, glass and filigree decoration, probably made between 1650 and 1750. With angels at the four corners and a cross in the centre, this small silver cover was designed to hold an Armenian Christian manuscript, such as a Psalter or a Gospel. It was almost certainly made in Isfahan’s New Julfa quarter. Forcibly resettling them from Julfa (Armenia) in 1604, Shah `Abbas developed this Isfahan suburb for a large Armenian population, allocating religious liberty, local self-government, interest-free loans and low tax rates.

Cpt_801.c: Walnut wooden book cover with ivory insets, made in the third or fourth century AD in Egypt. Some of the oldest known examples of wooden book covers are preserved in the Chester Beatty. This binding, cut from precious walnut, retains traces of leather as well as ivory insets carved with laurel ornament. The central panel (now missing) was also carved ivory and the visible damage to the walnut was probably a result of its forcible removal. Although the loss of this panel makes it impossible to know more about the book it once covered, such precious materials are a tell-tale sign of its luxury status. Book covers adorned with ivory, gold, silver and jewels are known as treasure bindings. While the oldest complete examples date to the fifth or sixth century, this ivory-inlaid cover, dated to the third or fourth century, may represent the earliest surviving treasure binding.

Cpt_802.c: Wooden board of cedar for a bookbinding with traces of leather and fragments of carved ivory insets, made in Egypt in the third or fourth century AD. Hollows in the shape of rosettes, now missing their insets, were probably the location of leather fasteners.

Cpt_803.c: Wooden board with leather filigree for a bookbinding dated to the 3rd century and made in Egypt.

Cpt_804.c: Pair of leather covered papyrus cartonnage boards for a bookbinding with fragments of reused parchment, made in Egypt between the fourth and seventh century AD. Fragments of parchment pages with Coptic writing still attached to the boards including a sheet reused as a paste-down. Fragments of textile lining as well as thread and leather thongs also preserved. Charring, discolouration and cracking of the in the leather are indicative of fire damage.

Cpt_806.c: Two cartonnage boards made from reused papyrus, from a bookbinding with fragments of leather, made between the 4th and 7th century in Egypt. The reused documents include Greek documentary texts. Fragments of three pieces of thread preserved in the second board.

Cpt_808.c: Leather and cartonage board with parchment lacing for a bookbinding made in Egypt between the 4th-7th centuries.

Cpt_810_1.c: One of a pair wooden boards with recess and carved decoration made in the 2nd or 3rd century AD in Egypt. These boards are among the early bindings published by Berthe van Regemorter (1879–1964) in 1958. The unusual interior hollows have led some to question whether these were in fact binding boards. Holes through the front and aligned along the edges, may have been used to attach the now lost textblock to the boards. Holes in the lower board retain fragments of leather thongs, while small pieces of metal in the holes along the spine edge were perhaps used to attach the covers to one another. The lower cover was repaired, probably at the time of its discovery in the early twentieth century, using sand and glue. The decorative crosses suggest a Christian purpose.

It was decorated with pen strapwork or interlace and cut into strips for attachment to the board. The wrapped bands were secured in place with the bone markers. In the 1930s, the original wrapping bands were carefully stored in card and glassine paper by Charles T. Lamacraft in London. However, this made them inaccessible. This work was conducted by the museum's Conservation team in 2022. This solution offers discrete and secure housing and enables safe display and access of the seventh-century wrapping bands.

Cpt_816.c: Parchment codex with a modern green leather binding preserving a lectionary (Katameros) written in Coptic and Arabic in the 16th century in Egypt. A lectionary is a book of biblical readings organised according to the liturgical year. The decorated frontispiece is a stepped-cross with interlace ornament flanked by four birds. The Alpha (Α) and Omega (Ω), or beginning and end, are written above and below the cross. The letters in the arms of the cross—ΙΗΣ ΠΧΣ ΧΣ ΘΣ—are abbreviations for the Coptic phrase Ⲓⲏⲥⲟⲩⲥ Ⲡⲓⲭ̀ⲣⲓⲥⲧⲟⲥ Ⲡ̀ϣⲏⲣⲓ ⲙ̀Ⲫ̀ⲛⲟⲩϯ (Iêsous Piekhristos Epshêri Emefnouti) or Jesus Christ, Son of God.

Cpt_818.c: Ostraca (broken piece of pottery) written in Coptic in the 7th or 8th century in Egypt. The text is an exhortatory tag probably written as a student exercise. ‘Blame no man, except that you have prayed... Be at peace with everyone in order that you might pray in Paradise (?). This is the Law of the Prophets.’ The staurogram became a standard opening to Christian documentary texts written in Coptic. A staurogram ⳨ is a Christian symbol derived from a ligature, the combination of two or more letters into a single glyph, in this case Tau (Τ) and Rho (Ρ).

Cpt_823.c: Folio from a Coptic manuscript, illuminated between the 3rd and 7th century AD in Egypt. Decorative border probably made with a compass. The descriptions of angels in biblical texts, however, are vague; they are described only as brilliant, fiery and shining. As a result, the appearance of angels in art had to be invented. The earliest representations of angels in Christian art show wingless figures. Winged angels only appear in the fourth century, their images derived from Roman Victories or winged genii (protective spirits).

Cpt_1494_1.c: Small papyrus scroll containing an archival copy of a homiletic letter from Horsiesios addressed to the brothers of the Pachomian monastic community in Egypt, written in Sahidic Coptic and probably copied in the seventh century. Horsiesios (d. 387) was successor to Pachomius, founder of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism, as head of the Pachomian Koinonia. This manuscript is associated with a collection of material from the Pachomian monastic library (also known as the Dishna Papers or Bodmer Papyri), a portion of which was purchased by Beatty in 1956.

Cpt_2013.c: Small parchment scroll (rotuli) containing an archival copy made for the Pachomian monastic library, probably at Phbow (Pbau), Egypt, of Theodore's Letter 2, on the annual remission of debts, written in Sahidic Coptic in the 6th century. Theodore (c. 314-386) was an early successor of Pachomius, the founder of Christian communal monasticism, as head of the whole community, centred at Phbow (modern Faw Qibla). The letter, entitled 'This is the letter from our father Theodore for the Remission', is a call to the annual meeting at the end of the year. It is associated with a collection of material from the Pachomian monastic library (also known as the Dishna Papers or Bodmer Papyri), a portion of which was purchased by Beatty in 1956.

Cpt_2022_1.c: Papyrus fragments preserving the Martyrdom of St Cephalon, an unknown Coptic martyr, executed under the prefect of Egypt, Clodius Culcianus. Text written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 6th or 7th century AD. Text on both sides (presumably continuous) suggests the fragment originally formed part of a codex. The text features the prefect presiding over the martyr's trial, Cephalon the martyr, and a third figure whose name is broken, perhaps Eusebios. (See also Cpt 2065)

Cpt_2026.t: Fragments of a homily or exhortation from an Easter Lectionary
Cpt_2026.c: Four papyrus fragments from a single folio, part of the Crosby-Schoyen Codex Ms 193. Written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt, and dated to the 4th or 5th century AD. The full codex contained Melito of Sardis' On the Passover, Jonah the Prophet, Jewish Martyrs, Epistle of Peter, and an unidentified homily or supplication for mercy. It has been suggested that the codex was an Easter lectionary composed at a Pachomian monastery. According to the editors, the codex originally contained 68 leaves (or 146 pages). These fragments are from the fifth and final text and are part of the same folio as Ms 193 p.127, containing text from the homily or exhortation. Both Moses and the Pharaoh figure prominently. This text may have been composed by Pachomius or one of his successors, Theodore or Horsiesius.

Cpt_2027.c: Papyrus fragment with non-biblical text about Pilate, written in Bohairic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2028.c: Fragments of papyrus folios which preserves text from the Martyrdom of Herai of Tamma, a twelve-year-old martyr. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. During the prefecture of Clodius Culcianus (c. 301-307 AD) a ship of Christian prisoners on route to trial at Antinopolis, dock at Tamma (Memphite) where Herai, the daughter of a presbyter, demands to be included among the prisoners. The prefect unsuccessfully attempts to dissuade her due to her age.

Cpt_2029_1.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus folios which preserve text from the Martydrom of Phoebammon, probably Phoebammon of Ausim (Letopolis). The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. Phoebammon was the grandson of Antichous, prefect of Egypt under Valerian. During the time of Maximian (r. 286-305 AD), after lengthy trials and tortures, Phoebammon was beheaded at Tam(m)a.

Cpt_2029_2.c: One of two frames containing fragments of two papyrus folios which preserve text from the Martydrom of Phoebammon, probably Phoebammon of Ausim (Letopolis). The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt. Phoebammon was the grandson of Antichous, prefect of Egypt under Valerian. During the time of Maximian (r. 286-305 AD), after lengthy trials and tortures, Phoebammon was beheaded at Tam(m)a.

Cpt_2030.c: Fragments of two papyrus folios containing passages from the Martyrdom of Hermauo. The text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2033_1.c: One of two frames containing eleven papyrus fragments which preserve text about Apa Pshoi of (the monastery of) Jeremias, an associate of Paul of Tamma(h). Text was written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 5th century AD, composed and/or copied by Ezekiel (perhaps the disciple of Paul of Tammah).

Cpt_2033_2.c: One of two frames containing eleven papyrus fragments which preserve text about Apa Pshoi of (the monastery of) Jeremias, an associate of Paul of Tamma(h).
