Cpt_2034.t: Homily on the weakness of the flesh
Cpt_2034.c: Papyrus fragment preserving a homily on the weakness of the flesh, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2036.c: Eleven papyrus fragments, some with Coptic text on both sides, some with text on one side only, and some blank, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments were written by at least four different scribes. Many appear to be Christian; one fragment mentions Abraham and God and another mentions a priest.

Cpt_2037.c: Eleven papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. At least three different scribes, and one fragment is written in a business hand.

Cpt_2038.c: Six papyrus fragments from two unrelated folios, with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment contains the words 'kingdom' and 'he blessed'.

Cpt_2040.c: Two unrelated papyrus fragments with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. One fragment mentions angel names and the other mentions the cross of Christ.

Cpt_2041.c: Two papyrus fragments from a literary codex with Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt (possibly Thebes). The larger fragment is paginated: Λ (30).

Cpt_2042.c: Sixteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments are probably all from the same papyrus manuscript or document.

Cpt_2043.c: Fifteen papyrus fragments with Coptic or Greek texts on one side only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2044.t: Papyrus fragments from Athanasius' letter to Dracontius
Cpt_2044.c: Nine papyrus fragments from a roll, with Coptic texts on the front only. The fragments preserve a portion of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius (see Cpt 2047), from a scroll in the Montserrat collection (P . Monts Roca inv. 14), written in Coptic in the 4th century in Egypt.

Cpt_2045.c: Nineteen papyrus fragments from a codex written in two columns, with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments include portions of the Passion homily (Peri Pasha) of Melito of Sardis, from what is known as the 'Crosby-Schoyen codex' (MS 193) (see Cpt 2046).

Cpt_2046.c: Twenty-four papyrus fragments preserving unidentified literary texts (most blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2047.c: Forty-seven papyrus fragments preserving some portions of Athanasius' Letter to Dracontius dated to the 4th century AD (see Cpt 2044) and other unidentified literary texts (many blank on the reverse), written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2048.c: Fragment of a papyrus folio from a codex, with Fayyumic Coptic text on front and back in two columns, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The text contains authoritative pronouncements about Sunday.

Cpt_2049.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a letter
Cpt_2049.c: Eight papyrus fragments written in Coptic cursive scribe on the front only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt, possibly preserving portions of a private letter.

Cpt_2050.t: Papyrus fragments possibly from a homily
Cpt_2050.c: Twenty-five papyrus fragments from a roll with Coptic text on the recto only, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. As Easter is mentioned the fragments may preserve part of a homily, perhaps Melito's Paschal Homily.

Cpt_2051.c: Two papyrus fragments with Greek and Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The upper fragment is written in Coptic and includes a gloss with 'faith, hope, charity' written in the upper margin and 'Moses, Solomon, David' in the left margin. The lower fragment is written in Greek, with different orientations on either side, 'Christ' is written on one and 'the kingdom of ... on earth' is written on the other side.

Cpt_2052.c: Papyrus fragments preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2053.c: Four papyrus fragments from two different folios preserving an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2054.c: Four papyrus fragments with Coptic and Greek texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Three fragments are written in Coptic including one with text from Mark 1.21, and one which is paginated; one fragment is written in Greek and mentions bread.

Cpt_2055.t: Parchment fragments from a homily citing Revelation 4
Cpt_2055.c: Fifteen parchment fragments with Coptic text on back and front, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve part of a homily citing Revelation 4; from a codex written in two columns. Evidence of damage from a fire.

Cpt_2056.c: Papyrus fragment from an unidentified literary text, written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt.

Cpt_2059.c: Twenty-three papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 8: 6.9-10, 14-15 and pagination; frag 6: 11.1-2, 6-7; frag 9: 11.49-52, 53-12.3 and 2 Corinthians (frag 2: 4.12-17, 18-5.4; frag 12: 6.17-7.4, 5-8), and pagination; and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2060.c: Twenty-one papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 21: 2:38, 43-44 and pagination; frag 10: 3.7-13, 14-4:2 and pagination) and pagination (frags 11 and 22), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2061.c: Thirty-one papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frags 17/13: 1.59-60, 61-62, 67-68, 68-69; frag 5: 2.38-39, 43-44; frags 1/7: 3.1-2, 5-8; frag 6: 5.10, 14; frag 8: 12.42, 47-48) and 2 Corinthians (frag 3: 2.15-16, 3.3-4; frag 2: 12.6-7, 10-12), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2062.c: Nine papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 7: 5.25-27, 30-32; frag 5: 9.18-19, 22; frags 2/4: 11.48-52, 53-12.3) and 2 Corinthians (frag 6: 5.10-11, 15-16; frag 1: 8.10-14, 14-20 and pagination); and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2063.t: Papyrus fragments including Luke 1.63, 1.70; 4.8, 13-15; 4.28-29, 34 and 2 Corinthians title, 1.1, 1.6; 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 11.22, 26
Cpt_2063.c: Fourteen papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve pagination and titling including portions of Luke (frag 9: 1.63, 1.70; frag 10: 4.8, 13-15; frag 13: 4.28-29, 34), pagination (frags 11 and 7) and 2 Corinthians (frag 12: title, 1.1, 1.6; frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frag 2: 11.22, 26), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2064.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 2.18-21, 23-25 and 2 Corinthians 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8
Cpt_2064.c: Four papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 2.18-21, 23-25) and 2 Corinthians (frag 4: 4.12-17, 4.18-5.4; frags 1 and 3: 6.17-7.4, 7.5-8), and are from a codex of the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2065.c: Papyrus fragments preserving the Martyrdom of St Cephalon, an unknown Coptic martyr, executed under the prefect of Egypt, Clodius Culcianus. Text written in Sahidic Coptic in Egypt and dated to the 6th or 7th century AD. Text on both sides (presumably continuous) suggests the fragment originally formed part of a codex. The text features the prefect presiding over the martyr's trial, Cephalon the martyr, and a third figure whose name is broken, perhaps Eusebios. (See also Cpt 2022)

Cpt_2066.t: Papyrus fragments of Luke 18.1-11, 13-15 and 2 Corinthians 3.7-13, 14-4.2
Cpt_2066.c: Two papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. The fragments preserve portions of Luke (frag 2: 18.1-11, 13-15) and 2 Corinthians (frag 1: 3.7-13, 14-4.2 with pagination), and are from a codex with the Gospel of Luke and 2 Corinthians (see Pap 2028 and Cpt 2024).

Cpt_2067.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Christian amulet with some Greek formulae as well as Coptic prayers, invocations to Gabriel and Iao and 2 wing formations based on Ablanathanalba and Achramachamari.

Cpt_2068.c: Papyrus roll preserving with Coptic magical texts on front and back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt. Probably a Christian amulet.

Cpt_2070.t: Papyrus fragment possibly from a letter
Cpt_2070.c: Papyrus fragment with Coptic text on both sides, possibly from a letter with the address on the back, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2071.c: About 38 papyrus fragments with Coptic text on front and back, probably literary texts, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 8th centuries in Egypt.

Cpt_2072.c: Thirty-eight mostly blank papyrus fragments made in Egypt, possibly from fragmentary Coptic manuscripts in the collection.

Cpt_2073.t: Papyrus fragments from the Acts of Peter
Cpt_2073.c: Seven papyrus fragments with Sahidic Coptic text on both sides, preserving part of the story of Marcellus from the Acts of Peter, undated but possibly written between the 4th and 6th centuries in Egypt.

Heb_752.c: Samaritan Pentateuch written on parchment by the copyist and liturgical hymn author Abisha ibn Pinhas ibn Joseph, dated 740 AH (1339-1340 AD), see folios 238-253. The text is arranged as a one-letter manuscript (with some instances of two-letter spacing), where justification was achieved by detaching a letter from the first and last words of each line. The manuscript retains notes from previous owners and deeds of sale on f.69: 23 Rajab 1308 AH (4 March 1891 AD), f.129: Jumada II 887 AH (July/August 1482 AD), f.169v: undated, two on f.227: Shawwal 844 AH (February/March 1441 AD) and 1308 AH (1890/1891 AD), and f.276v: 867 AH (1462/1463 AD). Signs of kissing are found on f.140v (Leviticus 9.22-10.1), f.179 (Numbers 6.21-23) and f.209v (Numbers 25.10).

Heb_753_1.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 4 bifolios (16 pages) containing Numbers 3.36–9.15, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_2.c: Fragment of a Samaritan Pentateuch comprising 3 bifolios (12 pages) containing Exodus 2.21–7.26, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last two letters from the final word of each line.

Heb_753_3_1.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 26.7–27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. It is a 'two-letter' type manuscript, where justification was maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_753_3_2.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Numbers 31.13–32.1, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Separator dots or colons appear at the end of almost every line and some separation of the letters occurs to maintain justification but it is not consistent.

Heb_753_4.t: Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_4.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Genesis 41.39–42.13 and 43.22–44.17, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification is achieved by detaching the first letter of the first word and the last letter or two of the final word of each line.

Heb_753_5.t: Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_753_5.c: Bifolio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Leviticus Leviticus 20.1–21.15 and 24.4–25.27, written on parchment and dated to between the 14th and early 16th centuries. Justification was achieved by detaching the first letter from the first word and the last letter from the final word of each line.

Heb_754.c: Folio from a Samaritan Pentateuch containing Exodus 8.2-9.17, written on parchment, in the 15th or 16th century probably in Palestine, Syria or Israel. Vertical and horizontal guide lines were impressed on the page to assist the scribe. It is a 'two-letter' manuscript, where symmetry is maintained by detaching two letters from the final word of each line to square the text.

Heb_755.t: Deuteronomy 9.7–11.12 and 12.17–14.28 from a Samaritan Pentateuch
Heb_755.c: Three bifolios (12 pages) from a single quire of a Samaritan Pentateuch containing portions of Deuteronomy written in Samaritan majuscule on paper, and dated to the 14th–17th centuries. The central bifolio (4 pages) of the quire is missing. The first letter of the first word and the last letter of the last word on each line is separated for text justification.

Heb_761.c: Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century. The combination of historic water and insect damage has caused the spine area to 'block' together into sections, leaving much of the manuscript inaccessible for handling, display and digitisation. However, folios 335-353, which were in better condition, have been fully conserved and are accessible (see Heb 761.1).

Heb_761_1.c: Folios 335–353 from a Hebrew Yemenite Pentateuch, with great Mazhor and small Mazhor, written on paper in Yemeni semi square script and dated to the 14th century.

Heb_762.t: Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital
Heb_762.c: Manuscript containing a Treatise on Astronomy (Sefer Ha-Tekhuna) by Hayyim Vital (1542–1620), written in Hebrew in a rabbinic script in Damascus in the early 17th century. It contains 17 diagrams in gold, red and blue, with titles in gold. Two previous owners signed the first folio: Raphael Mosche Galico and Hayyim de Rosa, both Jewish kabbalists based in Damascus in the 18th century. Hayyim Vital was a prominent kabbalist and the chief disciple of Isaac Luria in Safed (Israel), whose teachings are primarily known through Vital’s compendium, Etz Hayyim (Tree of Life). This treatise is one of Vital’s own works.

Heb_763.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with Ashkenazi traits and tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The parchment is divided into 'pages' with folds at regular intervals. The beginning of the roll is scalloped and tapers to a point with attached leather strap, but is otherwise undecorated. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_764.c: Festival prayer book (Mahzor) written on parchment in Hebrew in an Italian square script and dated to the 14th or 15th century, with an illuminated frontispiece and Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout. The lower border of the frontispiece contains an unidentified coat of arms of a lion or rampant on a field of azure.

Heb_765.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script, probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The beginning of the sroll is rounded and the other end is attached to a wooden roller. Each 'page' or column of text is decorated with a border painted with an orange pigment. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_766.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_767.c: Large portion of a Sefer Torah on vellum containing Genesis to Exodus 39, written in Hebrew in an Ashkenazic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 19th century. It retains one wooden roller.

Heb_768.c: Esther scroll (Megilat Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The 'pages' or columns of text are divided by painted borders. Its silver case is housed separately (Heb 768.1). The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_768_1.t: Silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah)
Heb_768_1.c: Embossed silver case for an Esther scroll (Megillah) probably made in Italy and dated to the 18th century. It is decorated with scroll work, floral design and an unidentified coat of arms ornamented with the 'hands of Cohen' and surmounted by a crown. The scroll was originally housed within the case, and when read was unfurled through the vertical slot then rerolled using the silver roller still attached to the scroll (see CBL Heb 768).

Heb_769.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th century. The very beginning of the scroll is not preserved. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_770.c: Esther scroll (Megalit Ester) written in Hebrew on parchment (sheep skin) in an Italian square script with tagin (crowns), probably made in Italy in the 18th or 19th century, attached to a single wooden roller. The Book of Esther recounts the story of the salvation of the Jews in the Persian Empire through the actions of the eponymous heroine. The text is read in synagogues on the spring holiday of Purim (Festival of Lots).

Heb_771_1.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer and two verses from Exodus (column 1: Exodus 13.1-10; column 2: Exodus 13.11-14; column 3: Deut 6.4-9 (shema), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_2.c: Small scroll on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deuteronomy 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment, while a head-tefillin/phylatery box contains fours biblical texts (Deuteronomy 6 and 11 and two passages from Exodus 13) each written on individual parchments; the arm-phylactery contains all four passages on a single parchment.

Heb_771_3.c: Mezuza ('doorpost') on parchment containing the Shema Yisrael prayer (Deut 6.4-9 and 11.13-21), probably dated to the 19th century. Traditionally, mezuzah scrolls include both Deuteronomy 6 and 11 on a single parchment.

Heb_772.c: Illuminated Hebrew Bible (Tanakh) on vellum, written in an Italian square script in Italy and dated to the 14th or 15th century, ornamented with Italianesque red and blue penwork throughout and bound in a contemporary leather binding. Bookplate of a previous owner, Baron Horace de Landau (1824-1903), on lower cover paste-down.

Heb_773.c: Almost complete Sefer Torah on parchment containing Genesis 21:10 to the end, written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script possibly in Italy, and dated to the 17th or 18th century.

Heb_774.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Deuteronomy 9:13-33:19 written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script, and dated to the 17th century.

Heb_775_1.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 1.1-31.19, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_775_2.c: Fragment of a Sefer Torah containing Genesis 10.21-14.10, written in Hebrew in an Italian square script in Italy in the 18th or 19th century.

Heb_776_1.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Leviticus written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the second portion containing Numbers 21.9-29.19.

Heb_776_2.c: Portion of a Sefer Torah on parchment containing Numbers 21.9-29.19 written in Hebrew in an Italian square script and made in Italy in the second half of the 18th century. The manuscript is preserved in two parts with the first portion containing Leviticus.

Heb_777.c: Sefer Torah on parchment written in Hebrew in a Sefardic square script in the 18th century.

Heb_778.c: A 19th-century book of remembrances or memorial book (Yizkor book) for the family of Judah ben Menahem. The title on the wooden cover says 'The Book of Life', a typical euphemism for a book commemorating the dead, with a crude carving of the tomb of Rachel. Ten members of the family are included, each with their name and date of death followed by longer Yizkor passages. Dates range from 1838 (Judah ben Menahem) to 1887 (Keyle Marcus). The illustration on f.1 is dated 1889.

Heb_779.t: Just measure (Kav ha-Yashar) and Orchard of pomegranates (Pardes Rimonim)
Heb_779.c: Paper folio with text written in Hebrew in an Oriental script, copied in the 18th or 19th century by a non-professional scribe in North Africa or the Middle East. The recto appears to be the title page for Kav ha-Yashar (Just measure) and a prayer from Pardes Rimonim (Orchard of pomegranates) is written on the verso. The title on the recto, ספר קב הישר (Sefer Kav ha-Yashar), is written beneath בשם רחמן (in the name of the Merciful One). Below this the scribe has written 'I am hereby beginning to write the Sefer Kav ha-Yashar, with the help of the Name (=God)', followed by a blessing on anyone who reads it (spelled incorrectly) and a curse on anyone who steals it. The drawing is probably a series of columns in emulation of contemporary printed-book title pages, with the beginning of the alphabet written in the damaged right-hand panel. Beneath the title for Kav ha-Yashar on the verso is a prayer from the Kabbalistic work Pardes Rimonim (An orchard of pomegranates).

Is_1401.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1401.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 20 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, with illuminated motifs (knots, stars, lobed medallions) as tenth verse counters throughout, sections from the Qur'an, suras 13:34 to 18:110 (but not continuous), probably Iraq, c. 800-900. Two other folios from this same dispersed manuscript are now in the Freer-Sackler museum in Washington, DC: F1929.72 and F1945.16.

Is_1405A.t: Two folios from the Blue Qur'an
Is_1405A.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1405A.c: Two folios from the Blue Qur'an. Codex, gold, silver and ink on indigo-coloured parchment, 2 folios in modern binding, Arabic text in black-outlined gold kufic script, with silver verse-markers within text and margin (fol. 1v), non-sequential text folios from the (dispersed) Blue Qur'an, Sura 2:60-65 (fol. 1) and Sura 2:93-101 (fol. 2), possibly Baghdad, Iraq (or Fustat, Egypt), undated, c. 775-850

Is_1405B.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1405B.c: Folio from the Blue Qur'an. Folio, gold, silver and ink on indigo-coloured parchment, Arabic text in black-outlined gold kufic script, silver verse-markers within text and margin (recto), from the (dispersed) Blue Qur'an, Sura 2:65-74, possibly Baghdad, Iraq (or Fustat, Egypt), undated, c. 775-850.

Is_1406.t: Illuminated folio, probably from a Qur'an
Is_1406.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1406.c: Illuminated folio, probably from a Qur'an. Single folio, colours and gold on parchment, horizontal panel of illumination, central roundel, eight-pointed star, and lightly-drawn backdrop of palmette-leaf trellis, with hasp ornament in the margin, possibly Syria or Iraq, c. 800-900

Is_1408.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1408.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, modern green silk-covered binding, 9 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, with sura heading (Sura 36, fol. 5v) in gold, and illuminated verse markers throughout, section from the Qur’an (Q35:33-36:17, missing one folio Q35:40-41), possibly from Juz'22 of a 30 volume set, unsigned, Iraq or Syria, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_1411.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1411.c: Folios from an `Abbasid Qur'an. The sura headings of this Qur'an manuscript are written out in gold script, with a large and colourful palmette design projecting into the margin for extra emphasis. There is a full page of illumination at the start and conclusion of the text, each in a different design of interlocking circles (at the start) and checkerboard (at the end). The layout is typical for a multi-volume Qur'an of this date, each separate volume would have splendid illumination panels, usually on facing pages at the beginning and at the end of the book. However this manuscript does not contain a complete "thirtieth" (juz') or "sixtieth" (hizb) of the Qur'an's full text, and is therefore a fragment of the original volume. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 11 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, sura headings in gold with large illuminated palmette, illuminated frontispiece (1v), finispiece (11r) and text markers throughout, final section of the Qur'an (sura 92:2- sura 114

Is_1414.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1414.c: Miniature Qur'an. Very small format Qur'ans are easily carried, and have long been used to provide personal protection to their owners in times of need, such as war or sickness. This small codex measures 9.6 x 5.9 cm, with thirteen clearly-written lines per page. Two notes have been added by later owners, recording the birth of sons, in the years 1011 and 1022: was this Qur'an kept close during childbirth? Codex, ink, colour and gold on parchment, 21 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, partial text of juz' 29 of the Qur'an (sura 71:3 to 99:98), with later notes added (to the inner covers) recording the birth of a son in 1011 (4 Jumada 402H), and again in 1022 (16 Shawwal 413H), possibly Iraq, undated, c. 800-900.

Is_1417A.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1417A.c: Juz' 3 of the Khayqani Qur'an. The Khayqani Qur'an is an important early example of the Arabic script known as "New Style" (also called eastern kufic), which developed gradually in Qur'anic calligraphy away from the more angular kufic script. This multi-volume Qur'an has been dated to c. 900 because of a note added to Juz' 19: on the final page is a statement in Persian, signed by someone called Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani. He notes that he has checked the text and made corrections, signing and dating his comment to the month of Sha`ban 292H (June 905). There have been doubts about the authenticity of this extra note, but not about the manuscript itself. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 47 folios, Arabic text in New Style III (aka eastern kufic) script, illuminated verse-markers, Juz' 3 of the Qur'an (2:253 to 3:91), from a thirty-volume set, of which Juz' 19 (CB Is 1417D) has a note signed al-Khayqani and dated 292H (June 905), probably Iran, c. 900

Is_1417C.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an

Is_1417D.t: Juz' 18 and 19 of the Khayqani Qur'an
Is_1417D.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1417D.c: Juz' 18 and 19 of the Khayqani Qur'an. The Khayqani Qur'an is an important early example of the Arabic script known as "New Style" (also called eastern kufic), which developed gradually in Qur'anic calligraphy away from the more angular kufic script. This multi-volume Qur'an has been dated to c. 900 because of a note added to Juz' 19: on the final page is a statement in Persian, signed by someone called Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani. He notes that he has checked the text and made corrections, signing and dating his comment to the month of Sha`ban 292H (June 905). There have been doubts about the authenticity of this extra note, but not about the manuscript itself. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 46 folios, Arabic text in New Style III (aka eastern kufic) script, illuminated verse-markers, Juz' 18 and 19 of the Qur'an (25:1 to 27:55), from a thirty-volume set, of which Juz' 19 (fol. 46v) has a corrections note in Persian signed Ahmad ibn Abi'l-Qasim al-Khayqani and dated

Is_1421.t: Three Folios from Juz' 17 of the Qur'an
Is_1421.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1421.c: Three Folios from Juz' 17 of the Qur'an, donated to the Great Umayyad Mosque of Damascus in 911. These are the last folios from a Qur'an manuscript, that was part seventeen of a thirty-volume set. As the text ended, the artist added a double page of illumination to conclude the volume. The final page records that the full thirty-volume set was donated to the congregational mosque in Damascus in the month Dhu'l-Qa`da in 298H, the equivalent date for July 911. Codex, ink, colours and gold on parchment, 3 folios, Arabic text in kufic script, illuminated double finispiece (ff. 2v-3r), final verses of Juz' 17 of the Qur'an (sura 22:77-78), waqf notice (f. 3v) of donation in Dhu'l-Qa`da 298H (July 911) to the congregational mosque of Damascus, naming the donor `Abd al-Mun`im ibn Ahmad, Damascus, Syria, 911.

Is_1425.c: Juz’ 18 of the Qur’an. a: Abu’l-Hasan `Ali ibn Hilal, known as Ibn al-Bawwab
Is_1431.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1431.c: The Ibn al-Bawwab Qur’an was produced in Baghdad in the year 1000. Its smooth cursive calligraphy is the work of Abu’l Hasan `Ali ibn Hilal (d. 1022), more commonly known as Ibn al-Bawwab (meaning "son of the doorkeeper"). Ibn al-Bawwab is renowned as one of Islam’s greatest master-calligraphers, and this manuscript is held to be the only Qur’an genuinely written in his hand. It is also important for being one of the earliest dated Qur’ans copied on paper (as opposed to parchment) and one of the earliest written in a cursive script. In the year 1000, Baghdad was ruled nominally by the `Abbasid caliphs, who were in turn controlled by the Buyid dynasty. While this Qur'an is not documented as a royal commission, Ibn al-Bawwab had connections to the Buyid rulers: before coming to Baghdad, he had served as chief librarian for a Buyid amir's collection in Shiraz, Iran. Is_1437C.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1437C.c: Partial copy of Juz' 30 of a Mamluk Qur'an. This Qur'an is written out in tumar script, as opposed to the more fashionable Mamluk scripts thuluth or muhaqqaq. The calligrapher has been identified as Ibn al-Wahid (d. 1311), a renowned practitioner born in Damascus in 1249, who studied under Yaqut al-Musta`simi (d. 1298) in Baghdad and settled in Cairo. Together with the master-illuminator Sandal, Ibn al-Wahid worked on a monumental Qur'an project (today in the British Library) for the Mamluk Sultan Baybars in 1306, and they may also have worked together on this manuscript. Much is recorded of Ibn al-Wahid's biography (and personality), including that he worked in Sultan Baybars' chancery, where the secretary complained of his negligence. However he was greatly admired for his calligraphic skill by the forgiving Baybars. The unusual use here of tumar (normally a chancery script) may further support the manuscript's attribution to Ibn al-Wahid. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 116 f

Is_1448.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1448.c: Juz' 12 of the Sinjar Qur'an. Written out in gold thuluth script, this manuscript is from a thirty-volume set, now dispersed in worldwide collections. The twenty-eighth volume (in the Khalili Collection, London) includes a statement on the original commission: the set was produced in 1211 (607H), for the library of one of the last rulers of the Zangid dynasty Qutb al-Din Muhammad, in Sinjar (northern Iraq). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, tooled leather bookbinding, 51 folios, Arabic text in gold thuluth script, with headings in gold eastern kufic script, illuminated frontispiece (fol. 1r) and finispiece (fol. 52v), Juz' 12 of the Qur'an (Sura 11:6 to 12:52) from a thirty-volume set made for the library (khizāna) of Quṭb al-Dīn Abū al-Muẓaffar Muḥammad ibn Zangī ibn Mawdūd ibn Zangī ibn Aqsunqur (r. 1198-1219), Sinjar, Iraq, 1211.

All five begin with the words al-hamdu li'llah ("praise be to God"). Folios (unbound), ink, colours, gold and silver (?) on pink paper, 61 folios, Arabic text in naskh script, with illuminated sura headings (fol. 31v) and verse markers throughout, extract from the Qur'an (suras 1, 6, 18, 34, 35 only), Iran, undated.

Is_1457_1.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex/Folio / Bi-Folio (Codex); Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1457_1.c: Folio from a Mamluk Qur'an. This single folio belongs to a codex (also in this museum: Is 1457I and II). Each side is beautifully illuminated, and each was created as a double page design: the geometric star design on the recto (here) would have faced an identical folio, which is now lost. As often with Qur'ans from Mamluk Cairo, the white kufic inscriptions at the top and bottom are different Qur'anic quotations, referring to the holy book itself: "Indeed We have sent [the Qur'an] down in a Night of Blessings" (Qur'an 44:3, top), and "Indeed We have sent down [the Qur'an] in the Night of Destiny (Laylat al-Qadr)" (Qur'an 97:1, bottom). On the verso, different illumination frames the first sura of the Qur'an. This text should face the second sura of the Qur'an, with matching designs: that opposite page remains in the codex (CB Is 1457I). Is_1476.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1476.c: Qur'an from Mamluk Cairo. This manuscript contains Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, and it was originally one of a thirty-volume set of the complete text. The opening folios present an illuminated double page, with matching panels of radial geometric design. The central octagons read "The Twenty-Seventh Juz'", in angular white kufic script. Set against gold ground, four lines of smaller text frame these central panels, with a Qur'anic quotation: "Truly this [Qur'an] is a revelation, From the Lord of the worlds, Which the true Spirit has brought down upon your heart, That you may be one of the warners, In clear Arabic language" (Qur'an 26:192-5). Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, 48 folios, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script, with sura headings in thuluth, and illuminated double page frontispiece (fols. 1v-2r), Juz' 27 of the Qur'an, illumination and calligraphy attributed to Ahmad ibn Kamal ibn Yahya al-Ansari al-Mutatabbib (unsigned), Cairo, Egypt, c. 1332-1336.

Is_1487.o: Approved Category 2017/Manuscript/Codex; Object by Function/Documents by function/Religious text/Qur'an
Is_1487.c: Juz' 7 of the Tarkān Khātun Qur'an. Codex, ink, colours and gold on paper, leather bookbinding with blind-tooling and gold detail, 109 folios, Arabic text in muhaqqaq script (thuluth and kufic for sura headings, thuluth in margin panels), with illuminated frontispiece (one half of a chahar-lawh double page, fol. 1r) and finispiece verse-markers and margin panels throughout, Juz’ 7 of the Qur'an (Sura 5:83 to 6:110), unsigned, northwestern Iran, c. 1175-1225, from a 30-volume set dedicated in 1288 by Qarākhiṭā’ī princess Bībī Tarkān in honour of her parents, Quṭb al-Dīn Muḥammad (d. 1257) and Qutlugh Tarkān Khātun (d. 1283), both rulers of Kerman.

Pap_1011.c: Christian amulet or magical text written in Greek on papyrus and made in Egypt probably in the 4th century. The horizontal breakage at regular intervals suggests the sheet was once folded or rolled. The amulet is composed of a serpent (or dragon) eating its own tail (οὐροβόρος) encircling an open bookroll filled with an eight-by-eight grid of Greek vowels. A bird at the top left holds a christogram (⳩) in its beak. The text on the serpent is a common magical palindrome, the final letters being ιαεω, the Greek magical rendering of the name Yaweh (with an additional letter). A tabula ansata (tablet with handles) hangs off the bottom of the serpent. The whole is surrounded by short names and phrases.

Syc_703.c: Harklean Gospels written in Syriac on parchment in Estrangela script by the scribe Isho’bar Romanos, completed in 1177 at the Church of the Holy Mother (Deipara Maria) situated near Tella d’Arsinos (modern Turkey). It was commissioned by the scribe’s uncle, Rabban Ahron, a priest and monk in Tella. The leather cover is ornamented with interlace borders, interlace cross on the front and an interlaced box on the back, possibly intended to represent the empty tomb. The Gospel book includes the Eusebian letter, canon tables, liturgical lessons, kephalaia (chapters), titles, colophons, and notes from the scribe. The canon tables, which occupy the first ten folios, are contained within architectural frames and decorated with a variety of birds, trees and flowers. This is followed by a stepped cross with interlace ornament and border, echoing the front cover. Square and circular interlaced medallions are found in the lower margin throughout. Syc_705.c: Parchment codex containing an evangeliary or the Nestorian lectionary written in the 12th or 13th century in Syria. It is written in the Estrangela script of Syriac with the title in Arabic on the back. It is bound with blind-tooled and stamped leather covers. Nearly every chapter is decorated with a coloured 'ribbon-over-a-rod' decoration in red, green and yellow.

Syc_709.t: Ephrem's Commentary on the Diatessaron / Letters: Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus (folios 1-10)
Syc_709.c: Parchment manuscript containing two distinct texts written in Syriac. The first ten folios reproduce an exchange of letters between Severus of Antioch and Julian of Halicarnassus relating to the corruptibility or incorruptibility of the body of Christ. It was written in a mixture of estrangela, nestorian and serta scripts in the 8th or 9th century in Egypt. The remaining sixty-five folios, also produced in Egypt, contain a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in estangela script and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. The two texts were acquired in 1957 and bound together in 1960. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists. Chapters 2.4-9.10 (with some lacunae) are preserved as CBL Syc 709.1. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Taken together, approximately 80% of the original codex survives (107 of the estimated 134 original folios). The Diatessaron w

Syc_709_1.c: Parchment manuscript containing a substantial portion of Ephrem's Diatessaron Commentary written in Syriac in estangela script in Egypt and dated to the late 5th or early 6th century. It was acquired in two parts, five folios in 1984 and a further 36 in 1986. This portion of the Commentary comprises chapters 2.4-9.10 (with lacunae at 2.15-20, 3.6-15, 4.2-6 and 7.25-27), the end of Matthew's infancy narrative to Jesus's meeting with Martha and Mary. Chapters 1.2-1.27, 9.14-18.3, and 21.4-22.5, prayers and a short section on the evangelists are preserved as CBL Syc 709. A single folio in Barcelona preserves 1.31-2.4. Taken together, approximately 80% of the original codex survives (107 of the estimated 134 original folios). The Diatessaron was a gospel harmony written by Tatian (120–173 AD), a second-century Christian theologian. W_022.c: Parchment codex containing the Old Testament books Genesis to Ruth written in Latin in black ink around 1153 for Walsingham Priory, Norfolk (England), around the time the monastery was founded. It is the first (and only extant) volume of a complete Bible. Initial letters are written in red, green or blue ink, some with additional pen flourishes. Important texts, rubrics and introductory words are written in alternating green and red. Marginal notes and corrections were added by a contemporary hand in brown ink. Some rubricator notes are still visible in the margins. Each book (or prefatory text) is illustrated with an historiated or decorated initial (10 in total). The manuscript was purchased by Edith Beatty in 1921 from Fitzroy Fenwick (Phillipps Collection 4769) as a gift for Chester Beatty. W_061.c: Bound parchment codex with leather cover preserving a Latin Psalter written in the 13th century in Flanders. The book includes a calendar, psalter, canticles, and litany. There are 12 calendar illustrations depicting abbreviated versions of the labours of the months, 14 full-page miniatures featuring scenes from the Life of the Virgin and the Passion of Jesus Christ, a full-page historiated Beatus initial with 9 additional historiated initials featuring saints, as well as various decorated initials. Each page has bar borders ending in human and animal heads, with other animals and figures in the margins.

W_080.t: Garden of knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia
W_080.c: Parchment codex containing Garden of Knowledge (Viridarium), a medieval encyclopaedia, primarily an edited version of Thomas de Cantimpré's On the nature of things (Liber de naturis rerum) with variations and interpolations (including quotations from Gervase of Tilbury), written, edited and illuminated by jurist Jean Reynaud between 1386-1425 probably in Avignon (France). Thomas de Cantimpré (1201-c. 1272) is best known for his encyclopaedia, compiled between 1230-1245, which purported to contain all the natural history knowledge of his time. It included information on anthropology, zoology, botany, mineralogy, astronomy, astrology and meteorology. Jean Reynaud's version took as his model a rare twenty-two book version of Cantimpré's encyclopaedia. The manuscript was purchased in 1924 from the Phillipps Collection.

W_082.c: Illuminated book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450), noted bibliophile and Admiral of France, on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457) and includes 148 three-quarter page miniatures painted in demi-grisaille. All but four were removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The manuscript includes a perpetual calendar, Gospel lessons, John's account of the Passion, Mixed Hours of the Virgin, Holy Cross and Holy Spirit, Penitential Psalms, Litany with prayers, Office of the Dead, Psalter of St Jerome, prayers to God, Christ, the Trinity, St Michael and the Holy Cross, Litany of Peter of Luxembourg, prayers to the Virgin in Latin and French, Suffrages, prayers to the Virgin and John the Baptist, a debate between Life and Death, and the Seven Articles of Faith in French. Beneath rubrics in red, the seventh lesson from Matins for the Office opens with the illuminated initial 'S' (Spiritus meus attenuabitur dies mei breviabuntur) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. Beneath rubrics in blue, the text opens with the illuminated initial 'Q' (Quicunque vult esse) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Trinity as three bearded men seated upon a throne supported by red seraphim and blue cherubim and/or thrones (both are among the highest order of angels). Each person of the Trinity touches the book with their left hand and gives a gesture of blessing with their right.

The fifth article of faith in French concludes on the recto, illuminated in the margins three figures emerging from flowers in prayer and a choir of angels playing viol, harp and psaltery. The sixth article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘A’ (A douques) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Ascension of Christ. Jesus’ ascension into heaven, his feet just visible, is witnessed by his mother Mary and the twelve apostles, probably John opposite Mary and possibly Peter behind her. W_082_f_356.t: Last Judgement from the Coëtivy Hours
W_082_f_356.c: Folio with three-quarter page miniature from a book of hours attributed to the Dunois Master, written in Latin and French in a bastarda script, made in Paris and dated 1443–1445. It was commissioned by Prigent de Coëtivy (1399?–1450) on the occasion of his marriage to Marie de Rais (1429–1457). The folio was removed from the bound volume between 1933 and 1960. The sixth article of faith in French concludes on the recto, illuminated in the margins by the rescuing of souls from hell. The seventh article of faith in French opens on the verso with an initial ‘C’ (Cest article) painted with white, red, blue and gold ivy-leaf ornament. The miniature is painted in demi-grisaille with pigments and gold and depicts the Last Judgment. Christ in a mandorla, displaying his wounds and flanked by trumpeting angels, sits on a rainbow as he watches over the rising of souls from their graves below. a: Bourdichon, Jean, attributed to; Fouquet, Jean, follower of; Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to; Master of Jean Charpentier, attributed to; Unknown
W_089.c: A Book of Hours written on parchment and illuminated between 1485-1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. The illuminations are attributed to at least five different hands: the Master of the Echevinage de Rouen (8), Jean Bourdichon (2), a follower of Jean Fouquet (6), the Master of Jean Charpentier (9), and the workshop of the Master of the Echevinage (calendar miniatures and secondary illumination). The pink velvet cover dates to a rebinding, probably in the 17th century. The link with Rouen is confirmed in the suffrages and litany, but not the calendar of feasts. Almost all folios with full-page miniatures were removed from the bound volume in the 20th century. The three miniatures that remain in the book are the Annuncation (f.35r), Harrowing of Hell (f.74r) and Ego sum (f.116v).

W_089_f_13.t: Four Symbols of the Evangelists from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_13.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The four symbols of the evangelists are depicted on a blue ground, each holding a scroll identifying their associated saint: the winged man (S. Matheus), the lion (S. Marcus), the ox (Sanctus Lucas), and the eagle (S. Iohannus). INICIUM SANCTI EVANGELII is written on the golden frame, decorated with acanthus scrolls. The text for the Gospel Lessons, beginning with John, continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains blue flowers.

W_089_f_16.t: Pietà from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_16.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. At the base of a T-shaped cross, a group of women and St John kneel, pray and grief around the body of Jesus which rests on the mantle of his mother Mary. John holds his head. A jar of anointing oils in the lower right is presumably included to identify one of the women as Mary Magdalene. A castle is depicted in the background. OBSECRO TE DOMINA is written on the golden frame, introducing a section of prayers to the Virgin. The rubic, 'cy ensuivent plusieurs honnes et devotes oroisons a nostre dame' is written on the recto below the concluding text to the Gospel Lessons (Mark) which finishes with a decorative line filler.

W_089_f_24.t: Tree of Jesse from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_24.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Jesse sits on a throne with a branching tree rising from behind him. This is a visual representation of the genealogy of Jesus, who depicted as an infant with his mother Mary above. The other ancestors are not identified but generally include Solomon and King David. LIBER GENERACIONIS IHESUS CHIRISTI is written on the gold frame. Lined only on the recto.

W_089_f_30.t: Christ taking leave of his mother from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_30.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The painting depicts Mary kneeling in prayer before a seated Jesus who holds an open book. A group of men are depicted in conversation in the background. The painting introduces the five prayers of St John the Evangelist to the Virgin, announced as Five Sorrows of the Virgin. The rubric on the recto reads, 'Cy ensuivent les cinq douleurs nostre dame contenants cinq resquestes'.

W_089_f_40.t: Visitation from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_40.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Mary stands in a landscape with her cousin Elizabeth who is pregnant with John the Baptist. She kneels as she recognises the significance of Mary's own pregnancy. A city with castle on a hill is depicted across a waterway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] MEU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Lauds of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorated initials introduce different sections of the text, one is decorated with a bird, the other with strawberries.

W_089_f_45.t: Nativity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_45.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. In a stable-like interior with stone walls and wooden roof, a haloed Mary knees before the infant Jesus, Joseph knees behind her. An ox and ass sit behind the infant. Several shepherds, including one playing the bagpipes, watch through windows and the doorway in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Prime of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one illustrated with a butterfly, the other with a bird.

W_089_f_47.t: Annunciation to the Shepherds from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_47.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. A night scene, illuminated by heavenly light from above and a camp figure below. A group of shepherds and shepherdesses in a landscape, some holding staffs and one playing the bagpipes, are visited by an angel announcing the birth of Jesus. A city is depicted across a waterway in the background. DUES IN ADIUTORIUM ME[EM] is written on the golden architectural frame, introducing Terce of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Prime of the Virgin. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one depicts a bird, the other a snail.

W_089_f_49.t: Adoration of the Magi from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_49.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Beneath a wooden-framed space, Mary sits with the infant in her lap, Joseph stands behind them. On the left side of the composition, three kings (one who has removed his crown) present gifts to the baby. A star is depicted in the upper left corner, with a riverscape in the background. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM MEUM is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words to Sext of the Virgin. The text on the recto concludes Terce of the Virgin and includes the rubric 'Ad Sextam.'

W_089_f_51.t: The Circumcision from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_51.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. Within an interior setting, a group of people crowd around a decorative table (altar). Mary and Joseph stand on the left while a male and female figure hold the infant Jesus as he is circumcised. DEUS IN ADIUTORIUM is written on the elaborate golden architectural frame. The text of None of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one with flowers the other with a bird.

W_089_f_53.t: Dormition of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_53.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The apostles stand and kneel around the deathbed of the Virgin Mary. Some hold their hands in prayer while others read from open books, including presumably Peter who also appears to be holding an aspergillum (instrument for sprinkling holy water). Another apostle holds a palm leaf, possibly John. The Resurrected Jesus stands with a staff, both his side and hand wounds visible, and offers a sign of blessing with his left hand. DEUS IN ADIUTORIU[M] is written on the golden architectural frame. The text for Vespers of the Virgin continues on the verso. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of the text, one encloses a small bird.

W_089_f_54.t: Coronation of the Virgin from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_54.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of Jean Charpentier. The Virgin Mary kneels as the Resurrected Jesus, wearing a purple cloak, places a crown on her head, signifying her role as Queen of Heaven. She kneels before God who is depicted as an old man wearing the papal tiara and seated in a covered throne. He holds the orb and cross (globus cruciger). The Holy Spirit in the form of a dove is depicted between God and Jesus. A choir of angels fill the background. CONVERTE NOS DEUS is written on the golden architectural frame, the opening words of Compline of the Virgin. The text on the recto includes the concluding prayers for Vespers of the Virgin and the rubric 'Ad completorium'. One two-line decorative initial contains flowers.

W_089_f_57.t: Man of Sorrow from a book of hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_57.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The resurrected Christ stands in his open tomb flanked by the Virgin Mary and St John. The composition may have been inspired by a print of the same subject by Martin Schongauer (1435/50–1491). Written on the bejewelled and gilded trompe-l'oeil frame, D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES, the opening words of Matins of the Holy Cross. The text continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials introduce new sections of text, one enclosing a small bird, the other two contain flowers.

W_089_f_59.t: Pentecost from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_59.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The Virgin Mary with a group of apostles and other women stand in a church-like setting as flaming tongues descend from the upper left. St James the Greater is identified by his pilgrim staff and scallop-emblazoned hat. D[OMI]NE LABIA MEA APERIES is written on the frame, which is decorated with a marble effect. The text for Matins of the Holy Spirit continues on the verso. Three two-line decorated initials open different sections of the text, each contain a small bird.

W_089_f_61.t: Deposition from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_61.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. STABAT MATER DOLOROSA is written on the golden architectural frame. Two men stand on ladders lowering the body of Jesus from the T-shaped cross, aided by a third man (perhaps Joseph of Arimathea) standing in front of the cross. Mary kneels in prayer, John holds the feet of Jesus and a woman (possibly Mary Magdalene) holds his hand. Three other figures are depicted in the background. The text, a hymn to Our Lady of sorrows, continues on the verso, each verse opens with a small decorative initial and each line is finished with decorative line-fillers.

W_089_f_65.t: Bathsheba bathing from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_65.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to Jean Bourdichon. Bathsheba is seen bathing in a fountain, with King David watching from the window of his castle in the background. DOMINE IN FURORE is written on the gold frame. The text on the verso is from the Penitential Psalms.

W_089_f_89.t: Three persons of the Trinity from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_89.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. The three figures of God the Father, Jesus and the Holy Spirit are seated in a triple niche with scalloped domes. The each hold an orb and cross (globus cruciger) in one hand and offers a blessing with the other. The central figure is winged. The whole setting appears to be floating. The golden frame is given a marble finish. The text on the verso begins 'Memoire de la benoiste trinite'. A second prayer 'Omnipotens sempiterne deus qui dedisti', opens with the Trinity within the historiated initial O. The text for 'De saint michiel archange' includes St Michael within an historiated initial D.

W_089_f_90.t: St Michael and the Devil from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_90.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. In a landscape, the armoured Archangel Michael fights two demons. One, trapped beneath his feet, attempts to bite the archangel's leg through his armour, the other clings to Michael's shield. No text is written on the golden framed, which is decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves, and therefore the opening words 'MICHAEL ARCHANGELE VENI' are missing from the following prayer. The text on the verso includes prayers to the Archangel Michael and the rubric, 'De monseigneur st michiel larchangel.'

W_089_f_91.t: Archangel Gabriel from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_91.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. The Archangel Gabriel, with bejewelled and billowing mantle, holds a cross and scroll which reads, 'Ave gratia plena.' He stands in a large gothic stone cathedral with groin vault. The golden tiles are decorated with blue letters. No text is written on the golden frame, and therefore the first words for the suffrage to the Archangel Gabriel are missing. The text on the recto includes the conclusion of prayers to St Michael and the rubric 'De saint gabriel larchange'. A two-line decorated initial depicts St Micheal.

W_089_f_93.t: St John the Baptist in the wilderness from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
W_089_f_93.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to a follower of Jean Fouquet. John the Baptist wearing his camel-hair tunic sits on a rock in a landscape with a sheep. He has a golden halo and holds a cross. PUER QUI NATUS E(ST) NOBIS is written on the bejewelled and gilded frame. The prayer on the verso opens 'Deus qui presentem diem hoborabilem.' St John the Baptist is depicted within the historiated initial D and St Peter is depicted in the historiated initial D, opening a prayer to 'De saint pierre'.

W_089_f_96.t: St George and the Dragon from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen
W_089_f_96.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St George, clothed in golden armour, sits on a white horse from which he slays the dragon. The bones of children the dragon has already eaten in the lower right corner. The princess, whose life is thus saved, stands on the left behind George, while the king and queen (her parents) watch from the top of their castle in the background. SALVE MARTIR GLORIOSE is written in the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Laurence and St Denis and the rubric, 'Memoire de saint george'. Two two-line decorative initials contain the gridiron of St Laurence and the beheaded head of St Denis.

W_089_f_100.t: Martyrdom of St Sebastian from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_100.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Sebastian, tied against a tree, is shot by two archers, multiple arrows already protrude from his body. A figure ties ropes around his feet. Three figures on the left direct the action against Sebastian. A stone, walled city is depicted in the background. O QUAM MIRA REFULSIT GRACIA is written on the golden frame, decorated with scrolling acanthus leaves. The suffrage to St Sebastian continues on the verso. A two-line decorative initial contains an arrow, the saint's attribute.

W_089_f_101.t: St Martin and the Beggar from a Book of Hours (use of Rouen)
a: Master of the Echevinage de Rouen, attributed to
W_089_f_101.c: Parchment folio from a Book of Hours written and illuminated between 1485 and 1490 in the Rouen workshop of the Master of the Echevinage, in collaboration with artist workshops in Tours. This illumination is attributed to the Master of the Echevinage. St Martin, sitting on a white horse before the gates to a city, uses his sword to cut his cloak. This is presents to 'the beggar', a man with crutch and wooden leg. Three angels and God hold scrolls written with prayers to the saint. O MARTINE O PIE QUAM PIUM is written on the golden frame. The text on the recto includes prayers to St Nicolas and St Germain and the rubric, 'Memoire de monseigneur saint martin'. Two two-line decorative initials introduce different sections of text, one contains St Nicholas.

W_094.c: A book of hours for the use of Paris in Latin and French, produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. It is written in a gothic script called ‘textualis quadrata’ using dark brown and red ink on parchment and bound in an 18th-century brown leather cover. There are 19 miniatures with realistically-rendered floral borders; 6 remain in the bound volume (ff. 1r, 3r, 11r, 12v, 17r, 23r). Eighteen folios, 14 miniatures (ff.4, 6, 7, 9, 14, 15, 19, 21, 25, 50, 69,126, 211, 242) and 4 text folios (ff.63, 68, 91, 98), were removed from the manuscript around 1954. The book was rebound in the eighteenth century, and pages were repaired and almost certainly removed at that time, likely in response to historic water damage (which is evident throughout the manuscript). A note in French on the fly leaf (f. iiiv), probably written around the time of the rebinding, records the prior removal of several folios with miniatures. W_094_f_04.t: March (recto), Hunting in April (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_04.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for March 15-31, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a particular saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St Benedict of Nursia (21 March) and the Feast of the Annunciation (25 March). On the verso is a hunting scene, introducing the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month,' here associated with April. The ivy-leaf borders are inhabited (in the upper margin) by two putti (wingless cherubs) fighting with shields. In the lower margin, a coat of arms is held between two eagles.

W_094_f_06.t: Enjoying in the Countryside (recto), May (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_06.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of a picnic, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', here associated with May. The borders are filled with realistically-rendered blue violets inhabited (in the upper margin) by a bird. In the lower margin, a coat of arms supported from a pole which rests on the shoulders of two putti (wingless cherubs), each standing on a short, four-legged stool. On the verso is the calendar for May 1-15, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week.
