W_094_f_07.t: May (recto), Hay Harvest in June (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_07.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for May 16-31, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St. Germain of Paris (28 May). On the verso is the hay harvest, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated with June. The border is filled with realistically-rendered holly, inhabited (in the upper margin) by an owl and a pair of water deities. In the lower margin, a coat of arms held by an angel.

W_094_f_09.t: Wheat Harvest (recto), July (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_09.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the wheat harvest, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', here associated with July. The border is filled with realistically-rendered strawberry plants, inhabited by birds, butterflies and putti (wingless cherubs). In the lower margin, a coat of arms held by an angel. On the verso is the calendar for July 1-15, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St. Martin of Tours (4).

W_094_f_14.t: Threshing, Selling and Sowing Seeds (recto), November (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_14.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of threshing and sowing seeds, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated here with November. The border is filled with realistically-rendered blue cornflowers, inhabited by butterflies and, in the upper margin, by a putto (wingless cherubs) with a spear facing a boar. In the lower margin, a coat of arms held between two squirrels. On the verso is the calendar for November 1-15, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here the Feast of All Saints (1), the F

W_094_f_15.t: November (recto), Fattening Pigs and a Banquet in December (verso), from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_15.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the calendar for November 16-30, divided into four columns. From left to right are (1) the Golden Numbers (Roman numerals used to calculate Easter), (2) the Dominical Letters (for identifying Sundays), (3) the Roman calendar days (Nones, Ides and Kalends), and (4) a saint or religious festival for each day of the week. The most important feasts are written in red, here St Clement of Rome (23), St Catherine of Alexandria (25) and St Andrew the Apostle (30). On the verso is a scene of fattening pigs and feasting, illustrating the seasonal activity, or 'labour of the month', associated here with December. The border is filled with realistically-rendered oak leaves and acorns, inhabited, in the upper margin, by a putto (wingless cherubs) holding a shield against a green lizard. In the l

W_094_f_19.t: St Matthew introducing the Gospel lesson of Luke, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_19.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Matthew seated on a canopied throne writing his gospel. His symbol, a winged man, holds the book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue and white columbines (Aquilegia) inhabited by butterflies. A putto with a spear and heron are in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held by two putti below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Luke and his name (lucam) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'In illo tempore, missus est angelus Gabriel a Deo in...' (At that time, the Angel Gabriel was sent of God into...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_21.t: St Luke introducing the Gospel Lesson of Matthew, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_21.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a portrait of Luke seated before a desk sharpening his pen, a scroll falls over the desk before him. His symbol, a winged ox, rests its hoof on a book. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted blue periwinkles (Vinca) inhabited by birds and butterflies. A putto and bear wrestle in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between two snails below. The portraits of Matthew and Luke incorrectly placed. Here the painting introduces the text for Matthew and his name (matheum) appears in red below. Three lines of text read 'Cum natus esset Iesus in Bethlehem Iuda...' (When Jesus was born in Bethlehem of Judah...). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_25.t: The Annunciation introducing Matins of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_25.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Annunciation. While Mary reads, the archangel Gabriel appears and announces her pregnancy. A vase of lilies rest on the floor between then. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted white lilies (Lilium), also known as the Madonna Lily. The tall stems of the flowers twist to create eight roundels in which prophets and ancestors of Mary are painted. The painting introduces Matins of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Domine labia mea aperies' (Lord, you will open my lips). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders.

W_094_f_50.t: The Visitation introducing Lauds of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_50.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Visitation. Elizabeth, pregnant with John the Baptist, embraces her also pregnant cousin Mary. They stand in a landscape, while Joseph walks out of the frame to the left. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted strawberries (Fragaria) inhabited by butterflies. A putto plays with a dog, while a cat hisses in the upper margin. The coat of arms is held between a dog and cat below. The painting introduces Lauds of the Virgin. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me). The text continues on the verso with more conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries.

W_094_f_63.t: Prime of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_63.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the verso is an historiated initial V with a half-length portrait of a man wearing an ermine-trimmed cloak. This is probably meant to represent King David, to whom the psalms are traditionally ascribed. The text which follows is from psalm 5, and begins Verba mea auribus percipe (Hear my words). The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains. The mound on the verso is home to a life-like rat.

W_094_f_68.t: Terce of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_68.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Hour of Prime of the Virgin, usually read around sunrise. On the recto is an historiated initial P with a half-length portrait of a nude woman. She is probably meant to represent Eve. The text which follows reads Paradisi porta per evam, and continues on the verso, cunctis clausa est. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders created with chains.

W_094_f_69.t: The Adoration of the Magi introducing Sext of the Virgin, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_69.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is the concluding text for the hour of Terce of the Virgin. The rubic for Sext of the Virgin (Ad vi) is written in red at the bottom. The text is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised strawberries. On the verso is a scene of the Adoration of the Magi. May holds the baby Jesus while a procession of figures on horses come to great them with gifts. The painting is surrounded by a border of realistically-painted boxwood leaves (Boxus) inhabited by butterflies. A dog faces a porcupine in the upper margin while two bears hold the coat of arms in the lower margin. The painting introduces Sext of the Virgin, usually read around noon. The three lines of text begin, 'Deus in adiutorium meum intende' (God, help me).

W_094_f_91.t: The Penitential Psalms, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_91.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Penitential Psalms. The recto includes text from psalm 50 which concludes on the verso. The is followed by the Latin word psalmus is written in red and the beginning of psalm 101; Domine exaudi orationem meum (Lord, hear my prayer). Both sides of the folio are decorated with conventional ivy-leaf borders and stylised flowers.

W_094_f_98.t: The Litany, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_98.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Litany, which includes invocations for the intercession of various saints. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains.

W_094_f_126.t: The Office of the Dead, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_126.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. The folio has text from the Office of the Dead. On the recto an historiated initial A contains a grotesque bird with leaves emanating from its beak. The text is from psalm 119 and begins Ad dominum cum tribularer clamavi (When I was in tribulation I cried to our Lord). The text continues on the verso. The borders are decorated with curving sprays of ivy which sprout from a yellow mound below. They are decorated with leaves and flowers in gold, and pale pink, yellow and blue. Acanthus leaves and suns in the same pale colours curve around vertical rods, and other borders are created with chains.

W_094_f_211.t: The Raising of the Cross introducing Sext of the Passion, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_211.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Raising of the Cross or Crucifixion. Jesus is nailed to the cross positioned diagonally across the picture as it is raised upright. The scene is crowded with soldiers and other onlookers. His mother Mary and friends grieve in the lower right. A ship sails on rough waters in the background. The painting is surrounded by blue larkspurs inhabited above by a putto facing a rearing long-horned goat. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two donkeys. The scene introduces Sext of the Passion (to be read at noon), and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers and acanthus leaves.

W_094_f_242.t: The Baptism of Jesus introducing a prayer to John the Baptist, from the Hamilton Field Hours
W_094_f_242.c: Parchment folio with pigments, ink and gold from the Hamilton Field Hours, a book of hours for the use of Paris produced between 1412 and 1420 probably in Paris by the Master of Walters 219. On the recto is a scene of the Baptism of Jesus by his cousin John the Baptist. Jesus stands in the Jordan River looking over his shoulder toward God who holds open a book. An angel looks down from mountains above. The painting is surrounded by pink roses inhabited by putti. In the lower margin, the coat of arms is flanked by two wildmen. The scene introduces a prayer to John the Baptist and continues on the back. The text on the verso is surrounded by conventional ivy-leaf borders with stylised flowers.

W_099.c: A rosarium codex written in Latin on parchment with miniatures painted by Simon Bening (1483-1561) made between 1540-1545 in Bruges. The codex is bound in a sixteenth-century Spanish gold-tooled leather binding with two metal clasps. A number of its miniatures were removed from the binding and are now housed separately. A rosarium is a collection of devotions dedicated to the Virgin Mary. One of the most conspicuous features of this richly illuminated example is its purple margins, a distinctive mark of royal ownership. Indeed, this illuminated rosarium was commissioned by either the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V (1500–1558) or his son, Philip II, King of Spain (1527–1598). The paintings are the work of Simon Bening, the last of the great masters of Flemish manuscript painting. Bening drew inspiration from his peers, quoting freely from Jan van Eyck and Albrecht Dürer, and he in turn influenced the next generation of artists. W_103_1.t: Calendar from the Chester Beatty Hours
W_103_1.c: Eleven parchment folios from the calendar of the Chester Beatty Book of Hours (February to December), created by the workshop of the Mazarine Master and completed in 1408 in Paris. The manuscript is one of the few securely dated Book of Hours (see colophon, W 103 f.158). All folios have fully illuminated foliate borders (water damage to all borders, especially September to December). Previous foliation (ff.169-178, with 2 folios numbered 171) from a historic rebinding. Miniatures had been removed from the manuscript and sold or otherwise dispersed in 1932, 1939 and 1969. The manuscript was further dis-bound following the Sotheby's sale on 24 June 1969 (lot 58).

W_116_1.t: Folio from the Chester Beatty Bible (Proverbs 31.5–Ecclesiastes 2.17), with Historiated Initial 'V'
W_116_1.c: Parchment folio from the Chester Beatty Bible preserving Proverbs 31.5–Ecclesiastes 2.17, written in Latin in a Gothic bookhand probably in Paris between 1250 and 1275 by the 'Dominican Painter'. The folio is ruled in plummet for two columns of 51 lines each. Capitals are stroked in red, rubrics and titles are written in red, and chapter numbers and running titles ('ECCASTES' and 'ECC') are written in alternating red and blue ink. The pages have clearly been trimmed, probably during a rebinding. The Book of Ecclesiastes is introduced by a ten-line historiated initial ‘V’ (verba) in blue on a red ground with white penwork, framed with a border in burnished gold with a foliate extension. It encloses the seated figure of King Solomon (commonly believed to be the author of Ecclesiastes). His lips are slightly parted as if about to speak. W_116_2.c: Parchment folio from the Chester Beatty Bible preserving Ezekiel 24.26–27.21, written in Latin in a Gothic bookhand probably in Paris between 1250 and 1275 by the 'Dominican Painter'. W_116_4.c: Parchment folio from the Chester Beatty Bible preserving 2 Timothy 2.12 to Titus 2.14, written in Latin in a Gothic bookhand probably in Paris between 1250 and 1275 by the 'Dominican Painter'. The folio is ruled in plummet for two columns of 51 lines each. Capitals are stroked in red, rubrics and titles are written in red, and chapter numbers and running titles ('Titum' ?) are written in alternating red and blue ink. The pages have clearly been trimmed, probably during a rebinding. The Epistle of Titus is introduced by a ten-line initial 'P' (Paulus) in blue with white penwork, gold frame and foliate extension. It encloses St Paul holding a sword. Smaller three- and five-line decorated initials are written in blue or red on a contrasting or gold ground with lacertine creatures or small animal heads, with white penwork, gold frames and bezants, and foliate extensions.

W_122.t: Dictys Cretensis' Trojan War (De bello troiano)
W_122.c: Illuminated parchment manuscript containing the fictitious eyewitness account of the Trojan War purportedly by Dictys Cretensis, written and illuminated by Bartholomew Sanvito in the mid to late 15th century in Italy. Each of the six books are introduced with decorative borders and the text includes a total of fifty-five miniatures painted primarily in blue or lilac camaïeu - a type of monochrome using a colour other than grey. The manuscript was made for Cardinal Francesco Gonzaga (1461-1483), whose arms appear on f. 3r. It was purchased by Edith Beatty in November 1925 from the Phillipps Collection and presented as a birthday gift for Chester Beatty in February 1926.

W_129.c: Small parchment scroll (rotuli) containing an archival copy made for the Pachomian Monastic Library, probably at Phbow (Egypt), of Pachomius' Letters 1-3, 7, 10 and 11a, written in Greek (translated from the Coptic original) in the fourth century. Pachomius (d. 346) is credited as the father of Christian cenobitic (communal) monasticism. He established the first monastery in Upper Egypt and the community quickly grew to 12 large monasteries housing thousands of monks. By the end of the fourth century sister communities had been established in Cappadocia, Syria, Palestine, Italy and Gaul. A collection of his writings and letters was probably assembled by his successors Theodore and Horsiesios. Many of the letters make a mysterious use of the alphabet, which may relate to the ancient Egyptian love of cryptograms, but efforts to decipher them have so far been unsuccessful. W_132.c: Parchment manuscript containing a twelfth-century copy in Greek of a series of homilies by John Chrysostom, John of Damascus, Anastasius Monachus, Hippolytus and others. Each homily is introduced with a decorative heading and an enlarged initial letter in red and blue. The title in the upper margin and rubrics also in red, passages identified by numbers in the margin (45–66). The first two folios and folios 11-15 are later insertions in a later hand. Green leather binding decorated with a gold tooled cross. The manuscript was purchased in October 1924 by John Hope Johnstone, on behalf of A. Chester Beatty, from the Russian Monastery of St Panteleimon (Rossikon) on Mt Athos.

W_133.t: Homilies of St John Chrysostom on the Gospel of John
W_133.c: Parchment manuscript containing a twelfth-century copy in Greek of a series of forty-six homilies (missing number 3) by John Chrysostom on the Gospel of John. An illuminated blue headpiece introduces the first homily, with each successive homily introduced with its number in the upper margin (*ΟΜΙΛΙΑ Δ* = Homily 4) and the passage from John under discussion followed by an enlarged initial letter, all in red. Red leather binding cover decorated with tooled gold cross. The manuscript was purchased in October 1924 by John Hope Johnstone, on behalf of A. Chester Beatty, from the Russian Monastery of St Panteleimon (Rossikon) on Mt Athos.

W_134.c: Manuscript containing the Four Gospels written in a 12th century Greek minuscule on parchment. Each gospel is introduced by a portrait of the Evangelist on a gold ground. Headpieces and initials are written in red ink with some penwork. A black-knotwork headpiece introduces the whole book. Rubrics indicating liturgical use appear in the margins.

W_139.c: Manuscript containing a Byzantine Gospel book written in Greek on parchment in the late 11th or early 12th century in modern Turkey or Greece. This deluxe gospel book was produced at the pinnacle of the Byzantine period and demonstrates a high degree of artistic and scribal mastery. Unusually, it retains a late-medieval binding with purple cloth covers, an indicator of its luxury status. Portraits of the evangelists and decorative headings are the focus of illustration and ornament in Byzantine gospel manuscripts. Here, St. Mark pauses from his writing to dip his pen in ink, with additional writing instruments and scrolls laid out on the desk and lectern before him. The gold background, symbolically placing him in a heavenly sphere, suggests divine inspiration. In addition to such rich illumination, the manuscript preserves almost every paratext (interpretation and commentary) found in gospel manuscripts up to this period in a highly developed form. W_142_1.c: Wooden writing tablet made in Egypt, dated between the 4th and 6th century AD. Three holes on one side for attaching to another tablet. An additional six holes were added at a later date to attach the two broken pieces together with thread. Unwaxed hollowed front preserves five columns of 'intermediate' Greek multiplication tables written with black ink. Leather residue on the back.

W_142_2.c: Wooden writing tablet, made in Egypt possibly in the 4th century AD. The central recess is waxed and preserves 13-14 lines of Greek script were written with a stylus. Four holes down one side of the frame were used to attach it to other tablets to create a notebook.

W_142_4.c: Wooden tablet with wax-filled hollow, made in Egypt probably in the early decades of the 4th century AD. A fragment of a leather thong in the bottom hole of W 142.6 was used to attach this board to three others to create a notebook. Greek note at the head of the tablet reads: 'Account of expenses 21st. For the harvesting of forty (40) talents'.

W_142_5.c: Wooden tablet with wax-filled hollow, made in Egypt probably in the early decades of the 4th century AD. A fragment of a leather thong in the bottom hole of W 142.6 was used to attach this board to three others to create a notebook.

W_142_6.c: Wooden tablet with wax-filled hollow, made in Egypt probably in the early decades of the 4th century AD. A fragment of a leather thong in the bottom hole was used to attach this board to three others to create a notebook. On the verso: the beginning of the Greek alphabet and four lines of illegible script which are probably Latin cursive. Tablet repaired in the British Museum in April 1948.

W_143_5_1.t: Folio with illuminated margins from a Greek Lectionary

W_147.c: Nikolje Gospels written on parchment in Old Church Slavonic in a Bosnian Cyrillic script with influence from the Raska School, made in Bosnia in the late 14th or early 15th century and probably a product of Royal Scriptorium of Tvrtko I (r. 1377–1391). Each of the four gospels is introduced by a miniature of the Evangelical symbol rather than a portrait of the author: winged man for Matthew (f.ii v), lion for Mark (f.46v), ox for Luke (f.79v) and eagle for John (f.136v). A headpiece (zastavki) with geometrical and vegetal ornament decorates the first page of text of each gospel, with a tail piece at the end of both Matthew and Luke. The headpieces for the gospels of Matthew and Mark include the Bosnian crown. Decorated initials are found on ff. 4v, 5r, 117r, 126r, 135r, 151v, 155r and 164v.

W_158.c: Parchment codex with leather cover containing a Lectionary in Serbian Church Slavonic, dated to the 13th century and attributed to the Raška school. The book contains prayers and the readings for eight Sundays after Pentecost, then for weekdays, martyrs, hierarchs, saints and the dead, Christmas, Epiphany and Sexagesima; it is incomplete.

W_159.c: A single illuminated paper folio preserving the opening of the Gospel of St Matthew in Church Slavonic, probably from a Gospel book, possibly made in the 15th century in Valahia or Walachia in modern Romania. A large headpiece (zastavka) is decorated with interlace branchwork (pletenka) and various decorative features including a bird, human hands, a serpent, cow's head, sun and moon. The decorated initial K, also created using interlace design, terminates in a manicule with two fingers pointing to the text. To the descenders of characters in the bottom line blossom into decorative ornaments.

W_173_3.t: Folio with St Peter in an historiated initial 'S' from the 'Chester Beatty Bible'

W_173_4.c: Parchment folio from the Mailhac-Faber Bible preserving Ezekiel 43.17–45.7, made in southern France in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century by an unknown French illuminator. From the second of a two-volume Bible (Isaiah to Apocalypse) of 286 leaves with 107 illuminated initials (76 historiated), now disbound and dispersed. Ruled in plummet for two columns of 40 lines each, written in brown ink in formal Gothic bookhand. Running titles ('EZE' and 'CHIEL') and chapter numbers in alternating red and blue ink (rubricator notes in margin). Two-line initials in alternating red and blue ink on contrasting purple or red penwork. Capitals are stroked in red and marginal corrections are circled in red. Penwork bar borders of alternately red and blue run the height of some columns and extend into the upper and lower margins with penwork.

W_173_5.c: Parchment folio from the Mailhac-Faber Bible preserving Ezekiel 45.7–47.6, made in southern France in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century by an unknown French illuminator. W_173_6.t: Folio from the Mailhac-Faber Bible (Interpretations of Hebrew Names) with Historiated Initial 'C'

W_173_6.c: Parchment folio from the Mailhac-Faber Bible preserving Jerome's the Interpretations of Hebrew Names in alphabetical order from Betharam to Capturi, made in southern France in the late thirteenth or early fourteenth century by an unknown French illuminator. From the second of a two-volume Bible (Isaiah to Apocalypse) of 286 leaves with 107 illuminated initials (76 historiated), now disbound and dispersed. Ruled in plummet for three columns of 47 lines each, written in brown ink in formal Gothic bookhand. Penwork bar borders of alternately red and blue run the height of some columns and extend into the upper and lower margins with penwork. Two-line initials are written in alternating blue and red ink on contrasting red or purple penwork. W_192.t: Wooton's Elements of architecture & Vitruvius' De architectura
W_192.c: Bound manuscript containing Henry Wooton's The Elements of Architecture (1624) followed by an incomplete English translation of Vitruvius' De architectura (30-15 BC), written and illustrated with architectural drawings by Michael Wills (active c. 1721-1777) in Ireland c. 1770. The texts are prefaced by a dedicatory letter by John de Laet to Queen Christiana of Sweden, dated Leyden, 15 May 1649. The gilt-featherwork binding is attributed to Edward Beatty (formerly known as Parliamentary Binder B), made in Dublin c. 1755.

W_195_097.c: Folio from a choir book with Jesus addressing three apostles in an initial E, introducing 'Ecce ego mitto vos' (Behold, I am sending you) from the first nocturne of the Common of Apostles, attributed to Neri da Rimini and produced in Rimini between 1300 and 1338 written in Latin with Gothic script.

W_195_098.t: Folio with St Paul in an historiated initial 'S' from an Antiphonary

W_195_099.t: Folio with Jesus in an historiated initial 'E' from an Antiphonary

W_195_117.c: Parchment folio from a choir book with historiated initial 'T'; probably made in Italy in the 14th or 15th century. The text from the initial reads 'Tolle arma tu[a pharetram et acrum]' (Take your weapons, quiver and bow). It is the beginning of the first response at matins for the second Sunday (Dominica Secunda) of Lent. The miniature within the initial shows Esau, with his quiver and bow, shooting a deer at the request of their father, Isaac.

W_222_1.t: Folio from the Grammont Abbey Bible

W_905.t: Ethiopian Psalter and Prayers to the Virgin (Weddase Maryam, Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay)
W_905.c: Parchment codex with blind-tooled leather covered boards and textile board linings of Indian ikat, containing a Psalter (ff.5v-130v), the Little Office of Mary (Weddase Maryam) (ff.131r-139r), malk'e (praise prayers) to the Virgin Mary (ff.2r-3r) and St Michael the Archangel (f.144r-146r), and additional praises and thanks to the Virgin Mary (Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay) (ff.139r-143v), written in Ge'ez and copied by 'Amda Masqal in the 19th century in Ethiopia for ወልደ ስማዕት (Welde Səma’etə), whose name appears on multiple pages. Interlace headings introduce prayers throughout the Psalter on ff. 5r, 11r, 17v, 24v, 33v, 40v, 46r, 54r, 64r, 71v, 76v, 88r, 99r, 101v, 107v; the first prayer to Moses on f.113r; the Song of Songs on f.124v; and the Lauds to Mary on f.131r. The name of ኃይለ መለኮት (Hayle Melekot), King of Shewa 1824-1855), for appears on f.143v.

W_906.t: Ethiopian Psalter and Prayers to the Virgin (Weddase Maryam, Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay)
W_906.c: Parchment codex with blind-tooled leather covered boards and textile board linings of a European printed cotton, probably originally in a handkerchief format, designed specifically for export, containing a Psalter (ff.6r-125v), the Little Office of Mary (Weddase Maryam) (ff.125r-134v), and additional praises and thanks to the Virgin Mary (Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay) (ff.135r-139v), written in Ge'ez in the 19th century in Ethiopia for ገበረ ሕይወት (Gəbərə Hiywet), whose name appears on ff.124v and 139v. Interlace headings introduce prayers on ff.6r, 39r, 79r, 107r, 118v, 125r, and coloured threads mark the start of important sections.

W_908.t: Ethiopian Psalter and Prayers to the Virgin (Weddase Maryam, Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay)
W_908.c: Parchment codex written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century, containing a Psalter, and at the end, a collection of prayers to Our Lady Mary, praises and thanksgiving to the Mother of God, and notes written in Amhairc. Decorative headings and bands on ff.1r, 7r, 13c, 14r, 21r, 31v, 39r, 44r, 51v, 61r, 68v, 74r, 86v, 97v, 100v, 106r, 112r, and 123v. The manuscript has a multi-colour, striped fabric binding cover with long straps. The leather satchel is housed separate (CBL W 908.1).

W_911.c: Parchment manuscript containing a series of prayers together with the gospels of Mark and John, written in Ge'ez and dated to the 19th century. It is illustrated with twelve full page paintings and five smaller paintings. Most of the texts are introduced with elaborate interlace headings (12 in total). Important sections are bookmarked with blue thread laced through the folios. The book opens with a pair of paintings depicting the Archangel Uriel with the Prophet Ezra facing a pair of saints, Abba Sehma and Akala Krestos (with a snake swallowing his beard). A hymn to the Virgin Mary closes with a portrait of the Virgin and Child. Prayers to the Trinity, lessons for each day of the week and "Sword of Divinity" prayer follow, interspersed with three paintings of saints. A portrait of St Mark introduces his gospel (with index). Prayers to St George are bookended with paintings of the saint, followed by a double-page painting of the Trinity facing the Archangels Michael and Gabriel. This i

W_914.c: Parchment codex with leather covers containing the Miracles of the Blessed Virgin Mary (Ta'amara Miriam) in Ge'ez, made in Ethiopian for Heraclius in the 18th century. The manuscript contains 48 full-page and three-quarter page paintings illustrating the various miraculous stories. The manuscript was once part of the collection of Lady Valeria Meux (1852–1910). It was later purchased by Chester Beatty at a Sotheby's sale on 14 June 1954 (lot 16).

W_916.t: Praises of Mary (Weddase Maryam) & Praises and Commendation to the Mother of Adonai (Weddase wa-genay la-Emma Adonay)

W_922.c: Parchment codex written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century, containing a text called Horologium (Mashafa Sa'ata), or 'The Clock' and a prayer to St John the Baptist on f.48v. The parchment of f.55 has been repaired with stitching. Fabric cover in red, black and yellow decorated with alternating decorative bands, the back board is short. Satchel is housed separately (CBL W 922.1).

W_922_1.c: Leather satchel for a parchment codex written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century, containing a text called Mashafa Sa'ata, or 'The Clock'.

a: Gebere Hiywet (ጸሐፍሁ ገብረ ሕይወት ); Welde Gebrael (ወልደ ገብርኤል)

W_930.c: Parchment codex with blind-tooled, leather covered boards and textile board linings of Indian ikat, containing the Homilies and Miracles of St Michael, written in Ge'ez and copied by ጸሐፍሁ ገብረ ሕይወት (Gəbərə Hiywet) (f.13r) and ወልደ ገብርኤል (Welde Gebrael) (f.73r) in the eighteenth century in Ethiopia. W_936.c: Parchment roll written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century, containing amuletic texts written for, and begins, 'Ta'os Azyos Masi Masyas Aqdefer. In the name of Haragu Harirekar. The text contains various passages from the Gospels concerning the expulsion of demons, followed by prayers of intercession to the Archangels Michael and Gabriel and the Nine Choirs of Angels, the Virgin Mary and lastly Alexander the Great. Five paintings depict, 1. a face enclosed in a cross shape with bands of eyes above and below, 2. a face imprisoned behind a cross shape, 3. a face enclosed in a cross shape with inscription, eyes in each corner, 4. a pair of lobed-shaped demons or serpents with inscription, and 5. a face enclosed in cross shape with checker-board patterns in the corners, birds at the top and bottom and an inscription above.

W_937.c: Amulet "magic" scroll or healing scroll (ketab) on two sheets of parchment, produced in Ethiopia in the 19th century. The name of the original owner (written in red) has been overwritten throughout with the name for a woman Wəltä Kidanə (ወለተ: ኪዳን). At the top it reads, 'for the protection of መጋኝ, ወሾተላይ, ዛር'. The text includes: 1. magical prayers against diseases; 2. "the words of the Angels Michael and Gabriel, Uriel and Cherubim, Raphael and Phanuel, Ariel and Raguel ... who stand before the Lord Almighty; 3. a prayer against the disease of Magdalene ...; 4. Solomon's (magical) names used to ensnares demons like fish in a net, and 5. a magical prayer that begins "In the name of God the Father, in the name of God the Son, in the name of God the Holy Spirit." There are three paintings: at the beginning a cherub with four sets of wings, in the middle a guardian angel with a sword, and at the end another cherub with four sets of wings. The last image includes the name of the woman: ወለተ: ኪ

W_938.c: Amulet "magic" scroll or healing scroll (ketab) on two sheets of parchment, produced in Ethiopia in the 19th century. The name of the original owner is erased but the feminine name ወለተ (Wəltä) is partly visible at the very bottom of the scroll. The text includes magical prayers: 1. 'Your Word is sharpened by the sword of your Word in the fire of faith'; 2. 'By these (magical) names of Jesus Christ ... let the unclean spirit be cut off and come out'; 3. the Litany of Jesus Christ; 4. a prayer; and finishes, 'By these (magical) names, may the spell of your servant be broken.' There are three illustrations: at the beginning is a geometrical pattern enclosing two faces, in the middle is another geometric pattern, and at the end is a crozier.

W_939.c: Parchment roll preserving magical prayers in Ge'ez, written in the 19th century in Ethiopia. The roll was used as an amulet or talisman and contains prayers and magic formulas including prayers against the evil eye and misfortune, and for strengthening the womb, as well as three protective paintings: (1) an archangel or guardian angel holding a sword, (2) a grid of nine squares with faces in the centre and corners, possibly the Net of Solomon for capturing demons, and (3) a face inside a star shape, possibly a cherub. Made for 'Ehta Maryam Terungo'.

W_940.c: Parchment roll preserving magical prayers in Ge'ez, written in the 19th century in Ethiopia. The roll was used as an amulet or talisman and contains Gospel passages (John 1.1-5 and Mark 8.28-32, Mark 1.23-28, and Luke 4.33-37) and magic prayers asking for relief from menstrual bleeding. There is one protective painting at the beginning of the roll: (1) a face inside an eight-pointed star or stylised wings, possible a cherub. Made for Walatta Giyorgis (erased: Negest Maryam) Milos Elyayas.

W_942_1.t: The Circumsion of Christ (recto), Simeon and the Infant Jesus (verso) from an Ethiopian prayer book
W_942_1.c: One of two detached folios from an Ethiopian prayer book illustrating, on the recto, the Circumcision of Christ and, on the verso, Simeon in the Temple recognizng Jesus as the messiah, painted and written on parchment in the 17th or beginning of the 18th century in Ethiopia and written in Ge'ez.

W_942_2.t: The Crucifixion (recto), The Resurrection (verso) from an Ethiopian prayer book
W_942_2.c: One of two detached folios from an Ethiopian prayer book illustrating, on the recto, the Crucifixion and, on the verso, the Resurrection, painted and written on parchment in the 17th or beginning of the 18th century in Ethiopia and written in Ge'ez.

W_949.c: Parchment codex with wooden cover (one broken board) containing a collection of Ethiopian hymns to various saints, written in Ge'ez in black and red ink and dated to the 18th century. An ink drawing of a figure is found on the last folio.

W_952.t: The Sword of the Trinity (Säyəfä Səlasse) and the Anaphora of Mary
W_952.c: Parchment codex with blind-tooled leather covered boards and textile board linings, containing the Säyəfä Səlasse ('The Sword of the Trinity'), intercessory prayers arranged according to the days of the week, and the Anaphora of Mary (Qǝddase Maryam), ascribed to Cyriacus, bishop of the city of Bahnasa, in Upper Egypt, written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the early nineteenth century for ክፍለ: ያዕቆብ 8s (Kilfe Yaqob), whose name appears on ff. 13r, 18r, 21r, 22v, 25r, 34v, 44v, 54r, 75v, 79r, 81v and 83r.

W_954.c: Parchment codex with blind-tooled leather covered boards and woven mashru textile (with silk warps and cotton wefts) textile board linings probably from India, containing an Ethiopian Psalter in Ge’ez with the Biblical Canticles (Mäḥalǝyä Näbiyat), the Song of Songs of Solomon (Mäḥalǝyä Mäḥalǝy zǝ-wǝ’ǝtu zä-Sälomon), the Praise of Mary (Wǝddase Maryam) and the Gate of Light (Anqäṣä Bǝrhan), copied by አለቃ ገበረ ሥላሴ (Aleqa Gebre Səlase) in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century.

W_955.c: Parchment roll written in Ge'ez in Ethiopia in the nineteenth century, containing prayers, the secret names of God and illustrations. Illustrations include 1. two standing figures with sword and cross, 2. four faces within a cross shape with checker-board patter corners, and 3. three standing figures wearing cloaks.

WX_04.c: Greek Icon on panel of the Virgin and Child of the Byzantine type known as the Hodegetria (She who shows the way). The thick primer applied and painted over to create patterns on the garments and haloes was possibly added later.

WX_05.t: Double-sided Icon: Madonna and Child (recto) and the Crucifixion (verso)
WX_05.c: Double-sided icon, the Virgin and Child painted with pigments on copper on the front is dated to the 18th-century Balkan Peninsula; the Crucifixion scene painted with pigments on the back was probably added later.

WX_37.c: Icon painting of a miniature iconostasis with Russian inscriptions, made in 18th century Russia.

WX_71.c: Wooden scribal palette with rectangular slots for holding reed brushes, made in Egypt before 100 AD. Some palettes were designed with a sliding cover. Many were also designed with two small oval wells at one end for black and red ink but here the scribe used the flat end of the palette to prepare black ink. The back has a sketch of a lion.

WX_72.c: Wooden scribal palette with rectangular slots for holding reed brushes, made in Egypt before 100 AD. Some palettes were designed with a sliding cover. Many were also designed with two small oval wells at one end for black and red ink but here the scribe used the flat end of the palette to prepare black ink.

WX_81_2.c: Hematite cylinder seal carved with a presentation scene and inscribed with the name 'Shamash' (name of the sun god), with modern impression, made in Babylonia during the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900-1600 BC).

WX_81_5.c: Hematite cylinder seal carved with standing figures and inscribed with the name of the owner - Iddin-Ea, son of Igmil-Erra, servant of Nergal', with modern impression, made in Babylonia during the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900-1600 BC).

WX_81_6.t: Cylinder seal: god pursuing a monster
WX_81_6.c: Chalcedony cylinder seal carved with an image of a god pursing a monster, with modern impression, made in Assyria during the Neo Assyrian period (c. 911-612 BC).

WX_81_7.t: Cylinder seal: worshipper and two scorpion men
WX_81_7.c: Chalcedony cylinder seal carved with a worshipper flanked by two scorpion-men and a dog, with modern impression, made in Babylonian during the Neo Babylonian period (c. 626-539 BC).

WX_81_8.c: Black stone cylinder seal with four animals, made in the Jemdet Nasr style (c. 3100-2900 BC).

WX_81_9.c: White stone cylinder seal carved with a contest scene of two crossed lions and two horned animals, made in Mesopotamia during the Akkadian period (c. 2350-2150 BC).

WX_81_10.c: White stone cylinder seal carved with a contest scene of one lions and two horned animals, made in Mesopotamia during the Akkadian period (c. 2350-2150 BC).

WX_81_11.c: Cream stone cylinder seal carved with a contest scene of two matching pairs - a hero and lion and a hero and buffalo - made in Mesopotamia during the Akkadian period (c. 2350-2150 BC).

WX_81_12.t: Cylinder seal: contest scene and presentation scene
WX_81_12.c: Hematite cylinder seal carved with a contest scene between a bull-man and lion and a presentation scene, made in Babylonia during the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900-1600 BC).

WX_81_13.c: Hematite cylinder seal carved with three deities, made in Babylonia during the Old Babylonian period (c. 1900-1600 BC).

WX_81_14.c: Milky quartz stamp seal carved with a winged Lamashtu, made in Assyria during the Neo Assyrian period (c. 911-612 BC).

WX_81_15.c: Chalcedony stamp seal carved with contest scene of a hero and bull, made in Babylonia during the Neo Babylonian period (c. 612-539 BC).

Wx_118.t: Portrait of King Louis XIV of France (obv) and Louis XIV receiving the Siamese ambassadors (rev)
Wx_118.c: Bronze medal commemorating the 1686 Siamese embassy to France designed by the royal medallist, Jean Mauger (1648–1722) and produced 1686-89 in Paris. A portrait of King Louis XIV (1638–1715) of France in profile is inscribed: LUDOVICUS MAGNUS REX CHRISTIANISS. On the reverse is an image of the French King receiving the Siamese ambassadors at Versailles, inscribed and signed: FAMA VIRTUTIS | ORATORES REGIS SIAM (Virtuous Fame, Ambassadors of the King of Siam), M. DC. LXXXVI. | MAUGER. F (1686 made by Mauger). The three Siamese ambassadors, Kosa Pan, Ok-luang Kanlaya Ratchamaitri, and Ok-khun Sisawan Wacha, kneel before Louis XIV and present a gift. The design may have been based on a drawing by Charles Le Brun (1619–1690) for a never completed painting. The reception was held in the Hall of Mirrors, attended by 1500 courtiers with Louis XIV seated on a silver throne raised on a platform draped with a Persian carpet.
